cards.claim: An EFS access point can enforce a user identity, including POSIX groups, for all requests made through it, and can enforce a different root directory so clients can access only that directory and its subdirectories.
cards.scope: EFS access point.

cards.claim: When you create an EFS access point you can configure an operating system user and group, and a root directory, for all connections that use it.
cards.scope: EFS access point.

cards.claim: If you specify the root directory's owner, EFS creates the access point root directory with the permissions you provide the first time a client connects.
cards.scope: EFS access point.

cards.claim: You can use IAM policies to enforce that specific applications use a specific access point.
cards.scope: EFS access point.

cards.claim: You use the EFS mount helper when mounting a file system through an access point, and the mount command includes the file system ID, the access point ID and the tls mount option.
cards.scope: EFS access point.

cards.claim: You must create at least one mount target in your VPC before using access points, because mount targets provide network connectivity while access points provide access control.
cards.scope: EFS access point.

cards.claim: Amazon EFS supports only advisory locking, and read and write operations do not check for conflicting locks before they run.
cards.scope: Amazon EFS file locking.

cards.claim: To support a broad set of NFS clients, Amazon EFS allows connections from any source port.
cards.scope: EFS mount target network access.

cards.claim: The EFS Archive storage class is supported on file systems with Elastic throughput, and if a lifecycle policy transitions data to Archive you cannot change the throughput mode to Bursting or Provisioned.
cards.scope: EFS Archive storage class.
links: [supported on EFS file systems with Elastic throughput](../facts/efs.md#efs-archive-needs-elastic-throughput-no-bursting-provisioned)

cards.claim: You can use the EFS mount helper or NFS to configure an EC2 instance to mount an EFS file system automatically when the instance starts.
cards.scope: Amazon EFS clients.

cards.claim: When you create a file system with the CLI or API, automatic backups are enabled by default only for One Zone file systems.
cards.scope: EFS automatic backups; default; adjustable.
links: [automatically backed up by AWS Backup by default](../facts/efs.md#efs-backup-cli-api-default-only-one-zone)

cards.claim: AWS Backup backs up all data in an EFS file system whatever storage class the data is in, performs incremental backups of EFS file systems, and restores all files to the Standard storage class when you restore a recovery point.
cards.scope: EFS backups with AWS Backup.

cards.claim: You can modify an EFS file system while a backup runs, but inconsistencies such as duplicated, skewed, or excluded data can occur if you make modifications during the backup.
cards.scope: EFS backups with AWS Backup.

cards.claim: When you create an EFS file system in the console, automatic backups are turned on by default.
cards.scope: EFS automatic backups; default; adjustable.

cards.claim: EFS Backups are enabled by default for all EFS One Zone file systems.
cards.scope: One Zone file system; default; adjustable.
links: [enabled by default for all EFS One Zone](../facts/efs.md#efs-backup-onezone-enabled-by-default-faq)

cards.claim: The default EFS backup plan and the default EFS backup vault cannot be deleted.
cards.scope: EFS default backup plan.
links: [backup plan and backup vault cannot be deleted](../facts/efs.md#efs-backup-plan-and-vault-cannot-be-deleted)

cards.claim: You can restore EFS backup data to either a new or an existing file system, and you can choose a full restore or an item-level restore.
cards.scope: EFS backups with AWS Backup.

cards.claim: By default, new EFS file systems do not allow public access, but you can modify file system policies to allow public access.
cards.scope: EFS block public access; default; adjustable.
links: [new EFS file systems don't allow public access](../facts/efs.md#efs-block-public-access-default-no-public-access)
[modify file system policies to allow public access](../facts/efs.md#efs-block-public-access-default-no-public-access)

cards.claim: Enabling Block Public Access protects EFS resources by preventing public access from being granted through the resource policies that are directly attached to the file system.
cards.scope: EFS block public access.

cards.claim: A file system with 100 GiB of metered data in Standard storage can burst to 300 MiBps read-only or 100 MiBps write-only for up to 72 minutes per day, and drive up to 15 MiBps read-only or 5 MiBps write-only continuously.
cards.scope: file system with 100 GiB of metered data in Standard storage, Bursting throughput; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: A file system with 10 TiB of metered data in Standard storage can burst to 3 GiBps read-only or 1 GiBps write-only for 12 hours per day, and drive 1.5 GiBps read-only or 500 MiBps write-only continuously.
cards.scope: file system with 10 TiB of metered data in Standard storage, Bursting throughput; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: A file system with 1 TiB of metered data in Standard storage can burst to 300 MiBps read-only or 100 MiBps write-only for 12 hours per day, and drive 150 MiBps read-only or 50 MiBps write-only continuously.
cards.scope: file system with 1 TiB of metered data in Standard storage, Bursting throughput; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: With Bursting throughput, the base throughput is proportionate to the file system's size in the Standard storage class, at a rate of 50 KiBps per each GiB of storage.
cards.scope: per GiB of Standard storage; fixed; not adjustable.

cards.claim: When burst credits are available, a file system can drive throughput up to 100 MiBps per TiB in Standard storage (100 KiBps per GiB), up to the AWS Region limit, with a minimum of 100 MiBps.
cards.scope: per TiB of Standard storage; maximum; not adjustable; burst credits available; up to the AWS Region limit.

cards.claim: With Bursting throughput, burst credits accrue when the file system consumes below its base throughput rate and are deducted when throughput exceeds the base rate.
cards.scope: EFS Bursting throughput.

cards.claim: File systems can accumulate enough burst credits to burst for up to 12 hours continuously.
cards.scope: EFS Bursting throughput; maximum.

cards.claim: File systems larger than 1 TiB can always burst for up to 50 percent of the time if they are inactive for the remaining 50 percent of the time.
cards.scope: Bursting throughput, file systems larger than 1 TiB; maximum; inactive for the remaining 50 percent of the time.

cards.claim: Total Bursting throughput for a Regional or One Zone file system in US East (Ohio), US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Sydney) and Europe (Ireland) is a maximum read of 5 GiBps and a maximum write of 3 GiBps.
cards.scope: per Regional or One Zone file system, for all connected clients, in the listed Regions; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: If no burst credits are available, a file system can drive up to 50 MiBps per TiB of storage, with a minimum of 1 MiBps.
cards.scope: per TiB of storage; maximum; not adjustable; no burst credits available.

cards.claim: Amazon EFS meters read operations up to one-third the rate of write operations, permitting a baseline rate of up to 150 KiBps per GiB of read throughput, or 50 KiBps per GiB of write throughput.
cards.scope: per GiB of Standard storage; maximum; not adjustable; Bursting throughput baseline.

cards.claim: Bursting throughput is recommended for workloads that need throughput that scales with the amount of storage in the file system.
cards.scope: EFS Bursting throughput.
links: [throughput that scales with the amount of storage](../facts/efs.md#efs-bursting-scales-with-storage-size-recommended-for)

cards.claim: The AWS case study says Ginkgo Bioworks is migrating to Amazon EFS, a serverless, fully elastic file system, to get more insight into its file usage and optimize further.
cards.scope: customer case study on the AWS site; a customer statement published by AWS, not a service guarantee.
links: [greater level of insight into its file usage](../facts/efs.md#efs-case-ginkgo-migrating-active-projects-to-efs)

cards.claim: The AWS case study says Mazzuma used Amazon EFS, a serverless, fully elastic file storage service, to store and transfer model data into Amazon SageMaker at speeds of 1.5 Gbps.
cards.scope: customer case study on the AWS site; a customer statement published by AWS, not a service guarantee.

cards.claim: The AWS case study says World Kinect, after migrating its Oracle E-Business Suite to AWS, used Amazon EFS to automatically provision and manage application files.
cards.scope: customer case study on the AWS site; a customer statement published by AWS, not a service guarantee.

cards.claim: On 2025-02-10 Amazon EFS raised the maximum number of access points a single file system can have from 1,000 to 10,000, and you can also request an increase for this limit.
cards.scope: access points per file system.

cards.claim: On 2023-11-26 Amazon EFS added the EFS Archive storage class, file system types, and the Transition into Archive lifecycle policy. EFS now offers three storage classes: EFS Standard, EFS Infrequent Access (EFS IA) and EFS Archive.
cards.scope: EFS storage classes.

cards.claim: On 2024-11-19 Amazon EFS added support for cross-account replication.
cards.scope: EFS Replication.

cards.claim: On 2026-07-28 AWS DataSync Enhanced mode began to support Amazon EFS and Amazon FSx for Lustre as source or destination locations. Before this, customers who wanted to move data to or from EFS or FSx for Lustre were limited to Basic mode.
cards.scope: AWS DataSync Enhanced mode locations.

cards.claim: On 2025-04-10 Amazon EFS raised the Elastic throughput read limit in all other Regions from 10 to 20 GiBps, while the specific Regions stay at 60 GiBps.
cards.scope: Elastic throughput read limit per file system, all other Regions.

cards.claim: On 2025-05-02 Amazon EFS raised the maximum read throughput for Elastic throughput file systems from 20 GiBps to 60 GiBps in Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Sydney) and Europe (London).
cards.scope: Elastic throughput read limit per file system, four Regions.

cards.claim: On 2023-04-13 Amazon EFS made Elastic the default and recommended throughput mode for file systems, instead of Bursting.
cards.scope: EFS default throughput mode.

cards.claim: On 2025-06-09 Amazon EFS added support for Internet Protocol Version 6 (IPv6) on the EFS service APIs and on mount targets.
cards.scope: EFS APIs and mount targets.

cards.claim: On 2024-05-15 Amazon EFS raised the maximum number of mount targets for each virtual private cloud (VPC) from 400 to 1,400.
cards.scope: mount targets per VPC.

cards.claim: On 2024-04-30 Amazon EFS set the maximum combined read and write throughput to 1,500 MiBps for file systems that use Elastic throughput and are mounted with version 2.0 or later of the EFS client (amazon-efs-utils) or the EFS CSI Driver (aws-efs-csi-driver).
cards.scope: per client, Elastic throughput.

cards.claim: On 2023-11-27 Amazon EFS made it possible to replicate file systems to existing file systems, which makes it easier to synchronize changes between file systems for failback purposes.
cards.scope: EFS Replication destination.

cards.claim: AWS recommends a current generation Linux NFSv4.1 client, such as those in the latest Amazon Linux, Amazon Linux 2, Red Hat, Ubuntu, and macOS Big Sur AMIs, together with the EFS mount helper.
cards.scope: Amazon EFS clients.

cards.claim: Amazon EFS provides the close-to-open consistency semantics that applications expect from NFS.
cards.scope: Amazon EFS.

cards.claim: Amazon EFS is accessible from most types of AWS compute instances, including Amazon EC2, Amazon ECS, Amazon EKS, AWS Lambda, and AWS Fargate.
cards.scope: Amazon EFS clients.
links: [most types of Amazon Web Services compute instances](../facts/efs.md#efs-compute-services-ec2-ecs-eks-lambda-fargate)

cards.claim: You can access an EFS file system concurrently from multiple NFS clients, and EC2 and other compute instances in multiple Availability Zones of the same Region can share it; EFS supports one to thousands of EC2 instances connecting at once.
cards.scope: EFS file system.
links: [one to thousands of Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) instances](../facts/efs.md#efs-concurrent-access-multiple-clients-multiple-azs)

cards.claim: For cross-account replication you must create both the source file system and the destination file system before you can create the IAM role for the source account; Amazon EFS cannot create the destination file system for you during replication.
cards.scope: EFS cross-account replication.
links: [cannot create the destination file system for you](../facts/efs.md#efs-cross-account-replication-destination-must-exist-first)

cards.claim: Cross-account replication needs an IAM role that gives Amazon EFS permission to replicate in the destination account, plus policies on the file systems that you share across accounts.
cards.scope: EFS cross-account replication.

cards.claim: For cross-account replication you must provide an IAM role when you create the replication configuration; using the service-linked role is not permitted.
cards.scope: EFS cross-account replication.

cards.claim: You can replicate EFS file systems across AWS accounts.
cards.scope: EFS replication.

cards.claim: You can use DataSync to transfer files between two EFS file systems, including file systems in different AWS Regions and file systems owned by different AWS accounts.
cards.scope: AWS DataSync with EFS.

cards.claim: AWS DataSync can copy data between NFS and SMB file servers, self-managed object storage, AWS Snowball Edge, Amazon S3 buckets, EFS file systems, and FSx for Windows File Server file systems.
cards.scope: AWS DataSync with EFS.

cards.claim: AWS DataSync provides a fast and simple way to securely sync existing file systems into EFS, and it works over any network, including AWS Direct Connect.
cards.scope: AWS DataSync with EFS.

cards.claim: AWS Direct Connect provides a dedicated network connection over which you can mount EFS file systems; once mounted, you can use DataSync to copy data into EFS up to 10 times faster than standard Linux copy tools.
cards.scope: AWS DataSync with EFS; maximum.

cards.claim: The AWS storage decision guide says file-based storage is mountable from virtually any operating system with the industry-standard protocols NFS and SMB, and that it suits workloads that need shared data across multiple compute instances.
cards.scope: file-based storage on AWS (EFS and FSx).
spoken: N F S and S M B

cards.claim: In the AWS storage decision guide table, block storage (Amazon EBS and the EC2 instance store) is for low-latency, high-performance durable storage attached to single Amazon EC2 instances or containers, such as databases.
cards.scope: storage type table of the decision guide.
links: [attached to single Amazon EC2 instances or containers](../facts/efs.md#efs-decision-guide-block-row-single-instance)

cards.claim: The AWS storage decision guide describes block storage as direct-attached to a compute instance with low-latency access, suitable for applications that need fast and consistent I/O.
cards.scope: block storage on AWS (EBS and instance store).

cards.claim: The AWS storage decision guide defines block storage as technology that controls data storage and storage devices.
cards.scope: storage type definitions.

cards.claim: The AWS storage decision guide defines file systems as storing data in a hierarchical structure of files and folders; in network environments, file-based storage often uses network-attached storage (NAS) technology.
cards.scope: storage type definitions.

cards.claim: The AWS storage decision guide defines object storage as technology that stores and manages data in an unstructured format called objects, where each object is tagged with a unique identifier and holds metadata that describes the content.
cards.scope: storage type definitions.

cards.claim: The AWS storage decision guide says that choosing a storage service with disaster recovery features, such as replication across multiple Availability Zones, can help minimize the impact of a disaster, and that you should weigh your recovery time objective (RTO) and recovery point objective (RPO).
cards.scope: disaster recovery criterion in the storage decision guide.

cards.claim: In the AWS storage decision guide table, file system storage is the type for applications that need shared read and write access across multiple EC2 instances or containers, or from multiple on-premises servers; the services listed for it include Amazon EFS and the Amazon FSx file systems.
cards.scope: storage type table of the decision guide.

cards.claim: The AWS storage decision guide says object storage gives access to data through an application programming interface (API) over the internet and is well suited to read-heavy workloads such as streaming applications and services.
cards.scope: object storage on AWS (Amazon S3).

cards.claim: The AWS storage decision guide lists things that can help you reduce cost when using an AWS storage service, among them: use the appropriate storage service for your workload type, and understand your data and how it is being used.
cards.scope: cost criterion in the storage decision guide.

cards.claim: The default EFS backup plan uses the AWS Backup recommended settings for automatic backups, which are daily backups with a 35-day retention period; you can edit the default backup plan settings using the AWS Backup console.
cards.scope: EFS default backup plan; default; adjustable.

cards.claim: By default, file systems that use Elastic throughput drive a maximum of 90,000 read IOPS for infrequently accessed data, 250,000 read IOPS for frequently accessed data, and 50,000 write IOPS.
cards.scope: per file system, Elastic throughput; default; adjustable; you can request an increase of up to 10 times these numbers.

cards.claim: The default EFS file system policy does not use IAM to authenticate and grants full access to any anonymous client that can connect to the file system through a mount target.
cards.scope: EFS file system policy; default; adjustable.

cards.claim: For most workloads AWS recommends the default modes, which are the General Purpose performance mode and the Elastic throughput mode.
cards.scope: EFS file system; default; adjustable.

cards.claim: You mount an EFS file system by its DNS name, which resolves to the IP address of the mount target in the same Availability Zone as your EC2 instance.
cards.scope: EFS mount target.
links: [resolves to the IP address of the EFS](../facts/efs.md#efs-dns-name-resolves-to-same-az-mount-target)

cards.claim: Elastic throughput is the best throughput mode for spiky or unpredictable workloads that are hard to forecast, or for applications that drive 5% or less of peak throughput on average.
cards.scope: EFS Elastic throughput.

cards.claim: Total default Elastic throughput for a Regional file system in US East (Ohio), US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Mumbai, Seoul, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo) and Europe (Frankfurt, Ireland, London) is a maximum read of 60 gibibytes per second (GiBps) and a maximum write (metered) throughput of 5 GiBps.
cards.scope: per Regional file system, for all connected clients, in the listed Regions; maximum; adjustable; increase through AWS Support.

cards.claim: Total default Elastic throughput for a Regional file system in all other AWS Regions is a maximum read of 20 GiBps and a maximum write (metered) throughput of 1 GiBps.
cards.scope: per Regional file system, for all connected clients, in all other Regions; maximum; adjustable; increase through AWS Support.

cards.claim: With Elastic throughput, EFS scales throughput up or down automatically, so you do not specify or provision throughput; you pay only for the metadata and data read or written, and you do not accrue or consume burst credits.
cards.scope: EFS Elastic throughput.

cards.claim: Elastic throughput is the default throughput mode in the Amazon EFS console and is recommended for most use cases.
cards.scope: EFS throughput modes; default; adjustable.
links: [default throughput mode in the Amazon EFS console](../facts/efs.md#efs-elastic-throughput-default-recommended)

cards.claim: Amazon EFS uses the industry-standard AES-256 encryption algorithm to encrypt data and metadata at rest.
cards.scope: EFS encryption at rest.

cards.claim: Encryption at rest is enabled by default when you create a file system in the EFS console, but when you use the AWS CLI, API or SDKs you must enable encryption explicitly.
cards.scope: EFS encryption at rest; default; adjustable.

cards.claim: Amazon EFS supports encryption of data in transit with Transport Layer Security (TLS).
cards.scope: Amazon EFS encryption in transit.

cards.claim: You can define service control policies in AWS Organizations to enforce Amazon EFS encryption for all accounts in your organization.
cards.scope: EFS encryption at rest.

cards.claim: After you create an EFS file system you cannot change its encryption setting, so you cannot make an unencrypted file system encrypted.
cards.scope: EFS encryption at rest.

cards.claim: In an encrypted EFS file system, data and metadata are encrypted before being written to storage and automatically decrypted when read, transparently to your applications.
cards.scope: EFS encryption at rest.

cards.claim: You can access EFS from containers launched by Amazon ECS, with both EC2 and Fargate launch types, by referencing an EFS file system in the task definition.
cards.scope: EFS with Amazon ECS.

cards.claim: You can access EFS from containers launched by Amazon EKS, with either EC2 or Fargate launch types, using the EFS CSI driver.
cards.scope: EFS with Amazon EKS.

cards.claim: You can access EFS from AWS Lambda functions by referencing an EFS file system in the function settings.
cards.scope: EFS with AWS Lambda.
links: [an EFS file system in your function settings](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-access-from-lambda-function-settings)

cards.claim: An EFS Access Point is a network endpoint that applications use to access an EFS file system and enforce file- and folder-level POSIX permissions, based on fine-grained access control and policy-based permissions defined in IAM.
cards.scope: EFS Access Points.

cards.claim: EFS Archive offers up to 50% lower cost than EFS Infrequent Access, with a higher request charge when the data is accessed.
cards.scope: EFS Archive compared with EFS IA; maximum.

cards.claim: EFS IA has no minimum storage duration; data tiered to EFS Archive has a minimum storage duration of 90 days.
cards.scope: per file, EFS IA and EFS Archive; minimum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: EFS Archive is optimized for and supported on EFS Regional file systems that use the default Elastic Throughput mode.
cards.scope: EFS Archive.

cards.claim: Amazon EFS Backup is powered by AWS Backup, which centrally manages and automates backups of EFS file systems.
cards.scope: EFS Backup.

cards.claim: During the initial backup of an EFS file system, a copy of the entire file system is made in the backup vault.
cards.scope: EFS Backup, AWS Backup vault.

cards.claim: You can access an EFS file system at the same time from on-premises servers and from EC2 instances in your VPC.
cards.scope: on-premises access to EFS.

cards.claim: You control which EC2 instances can access an EFS file system with VPC security group rules and IAM policies; security groups control network traffic and an IAM policy on the file system controls which clients can mount it and with what permissions.
cards.scope: Amazon EFS access control.
links: [Attach an IAM policy to your file system](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-control-instances-with-security-groups-and-iam)

cards.claim: For DataSync into or out of EFS you must first deploy a software agent, except when copying files between two Amazon EFS file systems.
cards.scope: DataSync with EFS.

cards.claim: DataSync can transfer files between two EFS file systems, including ones in different AWS Regions. AWS Transfer Family endpoints must be in the same Region as the EFS file system.
cards.scope: DataSync and Transfer Family with EFS.

cards.claim: Amazon EFS is designed to provide 99.999999999% (11 nines) of durability over a given year.
cards.scope: per year; fixed.

cards.claim: EFS provides a file system interface and file system access semantics such as strong consistency and file locking, with concurrently accessible storage for up to thousands of EC2 instances.
cards.scope: EFS.

cards.claim: The EFS FAQ says EFS is file storage for compute and on-premises servers, with strong consistency, file locking and concurrent access for up to thousands of EC2 instances; EBS is block storage for the lowest-latency access from a single EC2 instance; S3 is object storage reached through an internet API.
cards.scope: EFS, EBS and S3 compared.
links: [an internet API that can be accessed anywhere](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-efs-vs-ebs-vs-s3)

cards.claim: EFS file systems are elastic: they grow and shrink automatically as files are added and removed.
cards.scope: EFS file system.

cards.claim: The Elastic Throughput amount billed in a month is based on the read and write data transferred within the month, measured in GB transferred.
cards.scope: per month, EFS Elastic Throughput.

cards.claim: With Elastic Throughput, performance scales automatically with workload activity, and you pay only for the throughput you use, measured as data transferred per month.
cards.scope: EFS Elastic Throughput.

cards.claim: Elastic Throughput is the default throughput mode of EFS and is suitable for most file workloads.
cards.scope: EFS throughput mode; default; not adjustable.

cards.claim: Elastic Throughput is ideal when peak throughput is unknown or the workload is very spiky with low baseline activity, meaning it uses less than 5% of capacity on average when you provision for peak needs.
cards.scope: EFS throughput mode choice.

cards.claim: Amazon EFS can encrypt data at rest and in transit; the two can be configured together or separately.
cards.scope: EFS encryption.

cards.claim: Data encrypted at rest in EFS is transparently encrypted when written and decrypted when read, with encryption keys managed by AWS KMS.
cards.scope: EFS encryption at rest.
links: [Encryption keys are managed by the AWS KMS](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-encryption-at-rest-kms)

cards.claim: EFS encryption in transit uses industry-standard Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.2 between clients and file systems.
cards.scope: EFS encryption in transit.

cards.claim: Encrypting data has a minimal effect on EFS I/O latency and throughput.
cards.scope: Amazon EFS encryption.

cards.claim: After a disaster is over, you can fail back by transferring only incremental changes from the EFS replica back to the original file system.
cards.scope: EFS Replication failback.

cards.claim: An IAM policy attached to an EFS file system controls which clients can mount it and with what permissions, and EFS Access Points manage application access.
cards.scope: EFS file system policy.
links: [control which clients can mount your file system](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-file-system-policy-mount-permissions)

cards.claim: EFS Regional file systems (recommended) offer the highest levels of durability and availability by storing data with and across multiple Availability Zones.
cards.scope: EFS file system types.

cards.claim: The EFS FAQ says that, upon sign up, new EFS customers receive 5 GB of Amazon EFS Standard each month for one year under the AWS Free Tier, which is not applicable to files stored in the EFS One Zone file system type; the same FAQ says that starting July 15, 2025, new AWS customers receive up to $200 in AWS Free Tier credits that can be applied towards eligible services, including Amazon EFS.
cards.scope: new EFS customers, AWS Free Tier; EFS Standard only (not One Zone); The 5 GB offer is the FAQ's Free Tier wording; new AWS customers from July 15, 2025 receive Free Tier credits.
links: [5 GB of Amazon EFS Standard each month for one year](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-free-tier-5-gb-standard)
[not applicable to files stored in the EFS One Zone file system type](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-free-tier-5-gb-standard)

cards.claim: There is no minimum file size for IA or Archive, but files smaller than 128 KiB in these classes incur storage charges as if they were 128 KiB.
cards.scope: per file, EFS IA and EFS Archive billing; minimum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: Compared with EFS Standard, EFS IA and Archive offer the same throughput and IOPS scalability but with higher first-byte latencies.
cards.scope: EFS IA and EFS Archive compared with EFS Standard.

cards.claim: EFS IA offers up to 95% lower cost than EFS Standard for infrequently accessed data.
cards.scope: EFS IA compared with EFS Standard; maximum.

cards.claim: EFS Infrequent Access is designed for data accessed only a few times a quarter and EFS Archive for data accessed a few times a year or less, and both are cost-optimized classes with low double-digit millisecond latencies.
cards.scope: EFS storage classes.

cards.claim: In the EFS console you can apply common policies such as disabling root access, enforcing read-only access, or enforcing that all connections are encrypted.
cards.scope: EFS file system policy.

cards.claim: EFS Intelligent-Tiering promotes files from IA and Archive back to Standard when they are accessed, so later reads have the sub-millisecond latencies of EFS Standard.
cards.scope: EFS Intelligent-Tiering.
links: [back to EFS Standard when they are accessed](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-intelligent-tiering-promotes)

cards.claim: The default, recommended EFS lifecycle policy tiers files from Standard to IA after 30 consecutive days without access and to Archive after 90 consecutive days without access.
cards.scope: EFS Lifecycle Management; default; not adjustable.

cards.claim: Locking in EFS follows the NFS v4.1 protocol for advisory locking and lets applications use both whole file and byte range locks.
cards.scope: EFS file locking.

cards.claim: For Elastic Throughput, EFS meters metadata operations at a minimum of 4 KiB.
cards.scope: per metadata operation, Elastic Throughput; minimum.

cards.claim: EFS data transfer charges apply to metadata operations such as list (ls), remove (rm), and create directory (mkdir).
cards.scope: EFS Elastic Throughput billing.

cards.claim: Data can be encrypted in transit between an EFS file system and its clients by using the Amazon EFS mount helper.
cards.scope: EFS encryption in transit.

cards.claim: To access an EFS file system, you mount it on an EC2 Linux-based instance using the standard Linux mount command and the file system's DNS name.
cards.scope: EFS on EC2.

cards.claim: EFS uses the NFS v4 protocol.
cards.scope: EFS file access.

cards.claim: EFS One Zone file systems store data redundantly in a single AZ, so the data will be unavailable and might be lost during a disaster or other fault within that AZ.
cards.scope: EFS One Zone file systems.

cards.claim: EFS One Zone file systems support only one highly available mount target, in a single AZ.
cards.scope: EFS One Zone file systems; maximum.

cards.claim: EFS One Zone storage classes are ideal for workloads such as development, build, and staging environments.
cards.scope: EFS One Zone storage classes.

cards.claim: You mount an EFS file system on an on-premises Linux server with the standard Linux mount command, using the NFS v4.1 protocol.
cards.scope: on-premises access to EFS.

cards.claim: To access EFS file systems from on premises you must have an AWS Direct Connect or AWS VPN connection between the on-premises datacenter and your VPC.
cards.scope: on-premises access to EFS.

cards.claim: In the event of a disaster, you can fail over to the EFS replica file system and resume operations for business-critical applications within minutes.
cards.scope: EFS Replication failover.

cards.claim: If you interrupt EFS replication in a disaster recovery event, files that were transferred but not yet copied to their final locations are in a lost+found directory under the root directory of the replica.
cards.scope: EFS replica file system.

cards.claim: With EFS Replication you can configure the replica independently of the source to use cost-optimized storage classes and a shorter age-off lifecycle policy, to save up to 92% on costs.
cards.scope: EFS replica file system; maximum.

cards.claim: EFS Replication publishes a timestamp metric on Amazon CloudWatch called TimeSinceLastSync.
cards.scope: EFS Replication.

cards.claim: EFS provides the same file system access semantics, such as strong data consistency and file locking, across all EC2 instances and on-premises servers.
cards.scope: EFS.

cards.claim: EFS Standard is an SSD-powered class designed to deliver sub-millisecond latencies.
cards.scope: EFS Standard.

cards.claim: You can store petabytes of data in Amazon EFS.
cards.scope: EFS file system.

cards.claim: Amazon EFS offers three storage classes: EFS Standard, EFS Infrequent Access and EFS Archive, and EFS Archive is optimized for and supported on Regional file systems that use the default Elastic throughput mode.
cards.scope: EFS storage classes.
links: [EFS Standard, EFS Infrequent Access, and EFS Archive](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-three-storage-classes-standard-ia-archive)

cards.claim: EFS is a file storage service, Amazon EBS is a block-level storage service for use with EC2, and Amazon S3 is an object storage service.
cards.scope: EFS vs EBS vs S3.

cards.claim: The EFS FAQ says EFS supports big data and analytics, media processing, content management, web serving and home directories; Standard storage classes suit workloads needing the highest durability and availability, and One Zone storage classes suit development, build and staging environments.
cards.scope: Amazon EFS.

cards.claim: NFS client applications can use NFS version 4 file locking, including byte-range locking, for read and write operations on EFS files.
cards.scope: Amazon EFS file locking.

cards.claim: Every EFS file system has an automatically generated ID that is globally unique; file system names are tags and do not need to be unique, so they are not global like S3 bucket names.
cards.scope: Amazon EFS file system.

cards.claim: The AWS Free Tier is not applicable to files stored in the One Zone storage file system type.
cards.scope: One Zone file systems.
links: [is not applicable to files stored in the One Zone](../facts/efs.md#efs-free-tier-not-one-zone)

cards.claim: Max I/O performance mode has higher per-operation latencies than General Purpose mode, so AWS recommends always using General Purpose performance mode.
cards.scope: EFS performance modes.

cards.claim: You are billed for the amount of data in each EFS storage class, and you are also billed data access charges when files in IA or Archive are read or when data transitions between classes through lifecycle management.
cards.scope: EFS storage classes.

cards.claim: When you use IAM authorization for NFS clients, client connections and IAM authorization decisions are logged to AWS CloudTrail.
cards.scope: EFS IAM authorization for NFS clients.

cards.claim: You can use both IAM identity policies and resource policies to control client access to EFS, including read-only, write and root access.
cards.scope: EFS IAM authorization for NFS clients.

cards.claim: You must use the EFS mount helper to mount an EFS file system in order to use IAM authorization to control client access.
cards.scope: EFS IAM authorization for NFS clients.

cards.claim: You are not billed separately for IOPS on EFS; IOPS are included in a file system's throughput accounting.
cards.scope: Amazon EFS.

cards.claim: The EFS Infrequent Access (IA) and EFS Archive storage classes provide first-byte latencies of tens of milliseconds.
cards.scope: EFS IA and EFS Archive storage classes.

cards.claim: The EFS Standard storage class provides first-byte latencies as low as 1 millisecond for reads and 2.7 milliseconds for writes.
cards.scope: EFS Standard storage class; minimum; not adjustable; best case.

cards.claim: EFS lifecycle management automatically transitions data between storage classes according to the lifecycle configuration of the file system. The lifecycle policies apply to the entire EFS file system.
cards.scope: EFS lifecycle management.

cards.claim: By default, files not accessed in the Standard storage class for 90 days are transitioned into the Archive storage class.
cards.scope: EFS lifecycle policy, Transition into Archive; default; adjustable.

cards.claim: By default, files not accessed in the Standard storage class for 30 days are transitioned into IA.
cards.scope: EFS lifecycle policy, Transition into IA; default; adjustable.

cards.claim: By default, files are not moved back to the Standard storage class when they are accessed in IA or Archive; they stay in the IA or Archive storage class.
cards.scope: EFS lifecycle policy, Transition into Standard; default; adjustable.
links: [not moved back to the Standard storage class](../facts/efs.md#efs-lifecycle-default-no-move-back-to-standard)
[remain in the IA or Archive storage class](../facts/efs.md#efs-lifecycle-default-no-move-back-to-standard)

cards.claim: File system operations for lifecycle management have a lower priority than operations for the EFS file system workload.
cards.scope: EFS lifecycle management.

cards.claim: In the Amazon EFS console, Quick create uses recommended settings that include lifecycle policies to transition the file system to EFS Infrequent Access (IA) storage after 30 days, to EFS Archive storage after 90 days, and not to transition to EFS Standard storage.
cards.scope: per new file system, recommended settings; default; adjustable; console quick create.

cards.claim: EFS lifecycle transition time is based on when a file was last accessed in the Standard storage class, and the lifecycle timer is reset whenever a file in Standard is accessed.
cards.scope: EFS lifecycle management.

cards.claim: The lifecycle policy setting for the number of days after files were last accessed in the Standard storage class at which to move them to Infrequent Access (IA) storage (TransitionToIA) accepts AFTER_1_DAY, AFTER_7_DAYS, AFTER_14_DAYS, AFTER_30_DAYS, AFTER_60_DAYS, AFTER_90_DAYS, AFTER_180_DAYS, AFTER_270_DAYS and AFTER_365_DAYS.
cards.scope: per lifecycle policy; maximum; not adjustable; TransitionToIA.

cards.claim: For performance-sensitive use cases that need the fastest latency, such as applications with many small files, you can set the lifecycle policy to transition files back into Standard storage on first access.
cards.scope: EFS lifecycle policy, Transition into Standard.

cards.claim: The number of levels for directory depth in an EFS file system is 1,000.
cards.scope: per file system; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: File name length is limited to 255 bytes in an EFS file system.
cards.scope: per file name; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: The character limit for each EFS file system policy is 20,000.
cards.scope: per file system policy; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: The number of file operations per second for General Purpose mode is 250,000.
cards.scope: per file system, per second, General Purpose mode; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: The number of hard links to a file is 177 in an EFS file system.
cards.scope: per file; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: The number of locks on a single file across all instances and users is 512 in an EFS file system.
cards.scope: per file; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: Up to 65,536 active users for each client can have files open at the same time.
cards.scope: per client; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: For file systems using Elastic throughput and mounted with amazon-efs-utils version 2.0 or later or the Amazon EFS CSI Driver, the maximum combined read and write throughput for a Linux NFSv4.1 client is 1,500 mebibytes per second (MiBps).
cards.scope: per NFS client (Linux NFSv4.1); maximum; not adjustable; Elastic throughput; mounted with amazon-efs-utils 2.0 or later or the EFS CSI Driver.

cards.claim: For a Linux NFSv4.1 client, the maximum throughput for all file systems other than those using Elastic throughput with the newer EFS client or CSI driver is 500 MiBps.
cards.scope: per NFS client (Linux NFSv4.1); maximum; not adjustable; all other file systems.

cards.claim: The NFS protocol supports a maximum of 16 group IDs (GIDs) per user and additional GIDs are truncated from NFS client requests.
cards.scope: per user; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: Network latency of 1 ms or less is required to achieve maximum per-client throughput to EFS.
cards.scope: per client connection; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: Each unique mount on the client can acquire up to a total of 65,536 locks per connection.
cards.scope: per unique mount on the client, per connection; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: Up to 65,536 files can be open at the same time on the instance; listing directory contents does not count as opening a file.
cards.scope: per instance; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: Every Network File System (NFS) request is accounted for as 4 kilobyte (KB) of throughput, or its actual request and response size, whichever is larger.
cards.scope: per NFS request; minimum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: The size of a single file in an EFS file system is limited to 52,673,613,135,872 bytes (47.9 TiB).
cards.scope: per file; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: Symbolic link (symlink) length is limited to 4,080 bytes in an EFS file system.
cards.scope: per symbolic link; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: Max I/O performance mode is a previous generation mode and is not supported for One Zone file systems or for file systems that use Elastic throughput.
cards.scope: EFS performance modes.

cards.claim: File metadata, including file names, ownership information and the directory structure, is always stored in the Standard storage class.
cards.scope: EFS lifecycle management.

cards.claim: Metadata operations on files in IA or Archive storage, such as listing the contents of a directory, do not count as file access.
cards.scope: EFS lifecycle management.

cards.claim: With Elastic throughput, data operations are metered in 1 KiB increments after the first 32 KiB.
cards.scope: Elastic throughput, data operations; fixed.

cards.claim: With Elastic throughput, metadata operations are metered in 1 KiB increments after the first 4 KiB.
cards.scope: Elastic throughput, metadata operations; fixed.

cards.claim: Data access for IA and Archive storage is metered in 128 KiB increments.
cards.scope: IA and Archive storage classes, data access; fixed.

cards.claim: IA and Archive file metadata (2 KiB per file) is always stored and metered in the Standard storage class.
cards.scope: per file, IA and Archive; fixed.

cards.claim: Upon creation, a file system has a single empty root directory and therefore has a metered size of 6 KiB.
cards.scope: per new file system; fixed; not adjustable.

cards.claim: Each EFS file system object is metered for 2 kibibytes (KiB) of metadata (for its inode) and one or more increments of 4 KiB of data.
cards.scope: per object; fixed.

cards.claim: Amazon EFS meters file systems with Provisioned throughput mode enabled once every hour.
cards.scope: Provisioned throughput; fixed.

cards.claim: For file systems that use Provisioned throughput mode, you pay only for the amount of time that throughput is enabled.
cards.scope: Provisioned throughput.

cards.claim: Amazon EFS meters the throughput for read requests at one-third the rate of the other file system I/O operations.
cards.scope: read requests; fixed.

cards.claim: The EFS StorageBytes metric, the size of the file system in bytes including the data stored in the EFS storage classes, is emitted to CloudWatch every 15 minutes.
cards.scope: StorageBytes metric, per file system; fixed.

cards.claim: In the Total dimension of the EFS storage metric, the metered size of data stored in the file system in all storage classes, files smaller than 128KiB in the EFS Infrequent Access (IA) and EFS Archive storage classes are rounded to 128KiB.
cards.scope: StorageBytes metric, Total dimension.

cards.claim: The EFS Infrequent Access (IA) and Archive storage classes have a minimum billing charge per file of 128 KiB.
cards.scope: per file, IA and Archive storage classes; minimum.

cards.claim: AWS recommends the EFS mount helper for mounting EFS file systems on EC2 Linux and Mac instances; as an alternative you can mount manually with the standard Linux NFS client.
cards.scope: Amazon EFS clients.

cards.claim: When encryption of data in transit is declared as a mount option, Amazon EFS establishes a secure TLS connection when the file system is mounted, and all NFS traffic is routed through it.
cards.scope: Amazon EFS encryption in transit.

cards.claim: You can create a mount target when you create the file system or after, and later you can add mount targets, delete them, and change their security groups.
cards.scope: EFS mount target.

cards.claim: A mount target provides an IP address for an NFSv4 endpoint at which you can mount an EFS file system; to access a file system in a VPC you create one or more mount targets in that VPC.
cards.scope: EFS mount target.
links: [provides an IP address for an NFSv4 endpoint](../facts/efs.md#efs-mount-target-definition-ip-nfs-endpoint)
[one or more mount targets in the VPC](../facts/efs.md#efs-mount-target-definition-ip-nfs-endpoint)

cards.claim: You cannot change the IP address of an existing mount target; to change it you delete the mount target and create a new one with the new address.
cards.scope: EFS mount target.

cards.claim: To modify the VPC for mount targets you must first delete the existing mount targets.
cards.scope: EFS mount target.

cards.claim: EFS mount targets are designed to be highly available, and their IP addresses and DNS names in each Availability Zone are static even though they are redundant components backed by multiple resources.
cards.scope: EFS mount target.
links: [IP addresses and DNS for your mount targets](../facts/efs.md#efs-mount-targets-highly-available-static-ip-dns)

cards.claim: An EFS file system can have mount targets in only one VPC at a time.
cards.scope: EFS file system.

cards.claim: An NFSv4.1 client can only mount an EFS file system if it can make a network connection to the NFS port (TCP port 2049) of one of the file system's mount targets.
cards.scope: EFS mount target network access.

cards.claim: NFS client throughput is calculated as the total number of bytes that are sent and received, with a minimum NFS request size of 4 KB (after applying a 1/3 metering rate for read requests).
cards.scope: per NFS client; minimum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: You do not incur data access charges when you use AWS Backup to back up lifecycle-management-enabled EFS file systems.
cards.scope: EFS storage classes and AWS Backup.

cards.claim: You can create one mount target in each Availability Zone in a Region; if the VPC has several subnets in that zone you create it in one of them, and all EC2 instances in that zone share it.
cards.scope: EFS mount target, per Availability Zone.

cards.claim: One Zone file systems always use the General Purpose performance mode.
cards.scope: One Zone file system.

cards.claim: One Zone file systems that use Bursting throughput can drive the same per-file-system read and write throughput amounts as Regional file systems using Bursting throughput (maximum read of 5 GiBps for read and 3 GiBps for write).
cards.scope: One Zone file systems with Bursting throughput; maximum.

cards.claim: Total default Elastic and Provisioned throughput for a One Zone file system in all AWS Regions is a maximum read of 3 GiBps and a maximum write (metered) throughput of 1 GiBps.
cards.scope: per One Zone file system, for all connected clients, in all Regions; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: Amazon EFS automatically backs up One Zone file systems with AWS Backup, and you can restore a backup to any operational Availability Zone in the Region or to a different Region.
cards.scope: One Zone file system.

cards.claim: If all or part of the Availability Zone is lost or damaged, for example by fire or water damage, data in a One Zone file system may be lost.
cards.scope: One Zone file system.

cards.claim: When you use a One Zone file system with Amazon ECS, Amazon EKS or AWS Lambda, you need to configure the service to use the same Availability Zone as the file system: with Amazon ECS you should choose only subnets in that Availability Zone when launching your task, and with Lambda you configure your function to only launch invocations into subnets in that Availability Zone.
cards.scope: One Zone file system with ECS and Lambda.
links: [subnets that are in the same Availability Zone](../facts/efs.md#efs-onezone-ecs-eks-lambda-same-az-subnets)

cards.claim: EFS One Zone file systems are not resilient to a complete Availability Zone outage; during an outage you lose availability because the data is not replicated to a different Availability Zone.
cards.scope: One Zone file system.

cards.claim: One Zone file systems are available only in certain Availability Zones.
cards.scope: One Zone file system.

cards.claim: To mount a One Zone file system on an EC2 instance in a different Availability Zone, you have to specify the file system's Availability Zone name or the DNS name of its mount target in the mount helper command.
cards.scope: One Zone file system.
links: [DNS name of the file system's mount target](../facts/efs.md#efs-onezone-other-az-mount-needs-az-name-or-mount-target-dns)

cards.claim: Accessing a One Zone file system from an EC2 instance in the same Availability Zone as the file system's mount target avoids data transfer charges between Availability Zones and gives better performance.
cards.scope: One Zone file system.

cards.claim: A One Zone file system supports only a single mount target, located in the same Availability Zone as the file system; you cannot add additional mount targets.
cards.scope: One Zone file system.

cards.claim: You can mount EFS file systems on on-premises data center servers when they are connected to your VPC with AWS Direct Connect or Site-to-Site VPN.
cards.scope: Amazon EFS, on-premises access.

cards.claim: There is no additional cost for on-premises access to EFS file systems; you are charged for the Direct Connect connection to your VPC.
cards.scope: Amazon EFS, on-premises access.

cards.claim: To reach EFS from an on-premises server you add a rule to the mount target security group that allows inbound traffic to the NFS port (2049) from that server.
cards.scope: EFS mount target security group.

cards.claim: An on-premises server that mounts EFS must have a Linux-based operating system.
cards.scope: Amazon EFS, on-premises access.

cards.claim: AWS recommends mounting an EFS file system on an on-premises server by using a mount target IP address instead of a DNS name.
cards.scope: Amazon EFS, on-premises access.

cards.claim: By default the EFS mount helper uses DNS to resolve the mount target IP address, so when you mount from a different account or VPC you need to resolve the mount target manually.
cards.scope: Amazon EFS, cross-account or cross-VPC mount.

cards.claim: The AWS overview whitepaper describes Amazon EFS as a regional service that stores data within and across multiple Availability Zones for high availability and durability, and as fully managed with no changes needed to existing applications and tools.
cards.scope: Amazon EFS.

cards.claim: The AWS overview whitepaper says you can access EFS file systems across Availability Zones and AWS Regions and share files between thousands of Amazon EC2 instances and on-premises servers through Direct Connect or Site-to-Site VPN.
cards.scope: Amazon EFS.
links: [thousands of Amazon EC2 instances and on-premises servers](../facts/efs.md#efs-overview-thousands-of-instances-and-on-premises)

cards.claim: You cannot change the performance mode after the file system becomes available.
cards.scope: EFS performance mode.

cards.claim: Amazon EFS supports controlling access to file systems through Portable Operating System Interface (POSIX) permissions.
cards.scope: Amazon EFS.

cards.claim: If you access your EFS mount target from another AZ, you are charged the EC2 cross-AZ data transfer rate ($0.01/GB) for data transfer in and out of the AZ.
cards.scope: per GB, cross-AZ access to an EFS mount target.

cards.claim: AWS says you pay for EFS by the primary and backup storage you use and by your read, write and tiering activity. There is no minimum fee or setup charge.
cards.scope: Amazon EFS billing.

cards.claim: AWS says Elastic Throughput is the default throughput mode for EFS and is recommended for most workloads. With Elastic Throughput, performance scales automatically with your workload activity and you pay only for the throughput you use.
cards.scope: new EFS file systems; default; adjustable; throughput mode can be changed.

cards.claim: AWS says there are no data transfer charges when you access an EFS mount target from within the same Availability Zone, or when you replicate data across EFS file systems within the same Availability Zone.
cards.scope: EFS data transfer within one Region.

cards.claim: AWS says EFS One Zone file systems are ideal for applications that do not require the Multi-AZ availability and durability of EFS Regional file systems.
cards.scope: EFS One Zone.
links: [do not require the Multi-AZ availability and durability](../facts/efs.md#efs-pricing-one-zone-for-no-multi-az-need)

cards.claim: The Provisioned throughput amount billed in a month is based on the throughput provisioned in excess of the file system’s included baseline throughput from Standard storage, up to the prevailing Bursting baseline throughput limits in the AWS Region.
cards.scope: Provisioned throughput, per month.
links: [in excess of your file system’s included baseline](../facts/efs.md#efs-pricing-provisioned-excess-over-baseline)

cards.claim: AWS says to use EFS Provisioned Throughput if you have predictable and high levels of sustained throughput requirements, and that the amount billed in a month is based on the average throughput provisioned in excess of the baseline throughput included with your EFS Standard storage usage.
cards.scope: EFS Provisioned Throughput.
links: [predictable and high levels of sustained throughput requirements](../facts/efs.md#efs-pricing-provisioned-throughput-predictable-sustained)

cards.claim: AWS says that with EFS Replication you pay the prevailing storage and read, write and tiering activity rates for both the source and the destination EFS file system, plus any applicable data transfer charges between them.
cards.scope: EFS Replication billing.

cards.claim: Amazon EFS supports the Network File System version 4 protocol, in the versions NFSv4.1 and NFSv4.0.
cards.scope: Amazon EFS.

cards.claim: After you change a file system to Provisioned throughput or increase the provisioned amount, you must wait at least 24 hours before you can change the throughput mode again or decrease the provisioned amount.
cards.scope: EFS Provisioned throughput.

cards.claim: For file systems using Provisioned throughput, you are charged for the amount of throughput enabled for the file system.
cards.scope: EFS Provisioned throughput.

cards.claim: Total default Provisioned throughput for a Regional file system in US East (Ohio), US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon) and Europe (Ireland) is a maximum read of 10 GiBps and a maximum write (metered) throughput of 3.33 GiBps.
cards.scope: per Regional file system, for all connected clients, in the listed Regions; maximum; adjustable; increase through AWS Support.

cards.claim: Total default Provisioned throughput for a Regional file system in all other AWS Regions is a maximum read of 3 GiBps and a maximum write (metered) throughput of 1 GiBps.
cards.scope: per Regional file system, for all connected clients, in all other Regions; maximum; adjustable; increase through AWS Support.

cards.claim: With Provisioned throughput you specify a level of throughput that the file system can drive, independent of the file system's size or burst credit balance.
cards.scope: EFS Provisioned throughput.

cards.claim: Use Provisioned throughput if you know your workload's performance requirements, or if your application drives throughput at 5% or more of the average-to-peak ratio.
cards.scope: EFS Provisioned throughput.

cards.claim: To decide whether a file system policy is public, Amazon EFS assumes the policy is public and then evaluates whether it qualifies as non-public.
cards.scope: EFS block public access.
links: [assumes that the file system policy is public](../facts/efs.md#efs-public-policy-evaluation-assumes-public-until-fixed-values)

cards.claim: A file system can have a maximum of 10,000 access points unless you request an increase. Since February 10, 2025 the maximum is 10,000; it was 1,000 before.
cards.scope: per file system; maximum; adjustable; you can request an increase.

cards.claim: The number of connections for each EFS file system is 25,000.
cards.scope: per file system; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: By default, file systems that use Elastic throughput drive a maximum of 90,000 read IOPS for infrequently accessed data, 250,000 read IOPS for frequently accessed data and 50,000 write IOPS; if your workload requires more IOPS, you can request an increase of up to 10 times these numbers.
cards.scope: per file system, Elastic throughput; maximum; adjustable; request through quota increase.

cards.claim: The quota for mount targets is 1 mount target for each file system in an Availability Zone.
cards.scope: per file system, per Availability Zone; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: The quota is 1,400 mount targets for each virtual private cloud (VPC).
cards.scope: per VPC; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: The quota for security groups is 5 security groups for each mount target.
cards.scope: per mount target; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: The quota for tags is 50 tags for each file system.
cards.scope: per file system; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: The quota is 1 VPC for each file system.
cards.scope: per file system; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: EFS discounts read throughput so that you can drive higher read throughput than write throughput.
cards.scope: EFS throughput modes.

cards.claim: To mount an EFS file system from an EC2 instance in a different AWS Region than the file system, you must edit the region property in the efs-utils.conf file.
cards.scope: Amazon EFS, cross-Region mount.

cards.claim: EFS Regional file systems are designed to sustain data if an Availability Zone is lost, and they support concurrent access from mount targets in all Availability Zones of the Region.
cards.scope: Regional file system.

cards.claim: For a Regional file system a mount target is created in each Availability Zone, and AWS recommends that you access the file system through the mount target in the same Availability Zone for performance and cost reasons.
cards.scope: Regional file system; default; not adjustable.

cards.claim: A Regional EFS file system stores data redundantly across multiple Availability Zones in one AWS Region, which keeps the data continuously available even when one or more Availability Zones are unavailable.
cards.scope: Regional file system.

cards.claim: Regional is the recommended EFS file system type; it stores data redundantly across multiple geographically separated Availability Zones within the same AWS Region.
cards.scope: Regional file system.

cards.claim: When you enable replication, Amazon EFS automatically and transparently replicates the data and metadata of the source file system to a destination file system.
cards.scope: EFS replication.
links: [data and metadata on the source file system](../facts/efs.md#efs-replication-automatic-transparent-data-and-metadata)

cards.claim: Replication is available in all AWS Regions in which Amazon EFS is available.
cards.scope: EFS replication.

cards.claim: You cannot delete a file system that is part of a replication configuration; you must delete the replication configuration first.
cards.scope: EFS replication.
links: [cannot delete a file system that is part](../facts/efs.md#efs-replication-cannot-delete-file-system-in-configuration)

cards.claim: Deleting a replication configuration and changing the destination file system to be writeable can take several minutes, and you can delete the configuration from either the source or the destination file system.
cards.scope: EFS replication.

cards.claim: You can use EFS Replication to replicate your file system to a Region or Availability Zone of your choice, without managing additional infrastructure or custom processes.
cards.scope: EFS replication.

cards.claim: Amazon EFS does not create any mount targets when it creates the replication destination file system.
cards.scope: EFS replication.

cards.claim: To facilitate replication, EFS creates hidden directories and metadata on the destination file system, which equal approximately 12 mebibytes (MiB) of metered data that you are billed for.
cards.scope: EFS replication destination.

cards.claim: EFS Replication copies your file system data into a new or existing file system in the Region of your choice, transferring only incremental changes.
cards.scope: EFS replication.

cards.claim: The destination file system of EFS replication is read-only while replication is enabled, and applications can use it in read-only mode for low-latency cross-Region access.
cards.scope: EFS replication.
links: [use the replica file system in read-only mode](../facts/efs.md#efs-replication-destination-read-only-while-replicating)

cards.claim: During failback you can choose to discard the changes made to the replica during failover, or preserve them by copying them back to the primary file system.
cards.scope: EFS replication failback.

cards.claim: To fail over to the replica file system you delete its replication configuration; after the configuration is deleted the replica becomes writeable and you can use it in your application workflow.
cards.scope: EFS replication failover.

cards.claim: A file system can be part of only one replication configuration, and a destination file system cannot be the source of another replication configuration.
cards.scope: EFS replication.

cards.claim: Replicated data is accessible in the destination file system only after the initial sync completes, and how long that takes depends on the size of the source and the number of files.
cards.scope: EFS replication.

cards.claim: When you replicate to a new file system you choose the file system type of the destination, Regional or One Zone, and the KMS key used for encryption.
cards.scope: EFS replication.

cards.claim: EFS replication does not support using tags for attribute-based access control (ABAC).
cards.scope: EFS replication.

cards.claim: EFS replication is not point-in-time consistent: changes are transferred based on the Last synced time for the replication, and changes made to the source file system after the recorded time might not have been replicated yet.
cards.scope: EFS replication.

cards.claim: After the initial replication finishes, Amazon EFS maintains a recovery point objective (RPO) of 15 minutes for most file systems.
cards.scope: EFS replication, after initial sync.

cards.claim: If the source file system has files that change very frequently and has either more than 100 million files or files larger than 100 GB, replication may take longer than 15 minutes.
cards.scope: EFS replication.

cards.claim: EFS replication is continual and designed to provide a recovery point objective (RPO) and a recovery time objective (RTO) of minutes.
cards.scope: EFS replication.

cards.claim: You can access training data in EFS from Amazon SageMaker training jobs by referencing an EFS file system in your CreateTrainingJob request.
cards.scope: Amazon EFS with SageMaker.

cards.claim: NFS client access to Amazon EFS is controlled by both IAM policies and network security policies such as security groups. EFS also supports controlling access through POSIX permissions.
cards.scope: Amazon EFS.
links: [controlled by both AWS Identity and Access Management](../facts/efs.md#efs-security-access-iam-and-security-groups)

cards.claim: When using EFS you specify VPC security groups for your EC2 instances and security groups for the EFS mount targets associated with the file system.
cards.scope: EFS mount target network access.

cards.claim: Amazon EFS is serverless and fully elastic: you do not provision or manage storage capacity, and a file system grows and shrinks automatically as you add and remove files.
cards.scope: Amazon EFS file system.

cards.claim: Under the Amazon EFS SLA, for file systems using One Zone storage classes, a Monthly Uptime Percentage less than 99.9% but greater than or equal to 99.0% earns a 10% service credit.
cards.scope: per file system, One Zone storage classes, Monthly Uptime Percentage.

cards.claim: Under the Amazon EFS SLA, for file systems using Standard storage classes, a Monthly Uptime Percentage less than 99.99% but greater than or equal to 99.0% earns a 10% service credit.
cards.scope: per file system, Standard storage classes, Monthly Uptime Percentage.

cards.claim: In the file system types table, the Regional file system type is listed with an availability of 99.99% across at least 3 Availability Zones.
cards.scope: Regional file systems; as listed in the file system types table.

cards.claim: The EFS Standard storage class uses SSD storage for the lowest latency for frequently accessed files, and new file system data is written to Standard first before lifecycle management can tier it to IA or Archive.
cards.scope: EFS storage classes.
links: [first written to the EFS Standard storage class](../facts/efs.md#efs-standard-class-ssd-lowest-latency-new-data-first)

cards.claim: You can change the throughput mode and the provisioned throughput amount after the file system is available, and changing the throughput mode does not cause application downtime.
cards.scope: EFS throughput modes.

cards.claim: Amazon EFS offers three throughput modes: Elastic, Provisioned, and Bursting.
cards.scope: EFS throughput modes.

cards.claim: Throughput in excess of an AWS Region's maximum throughput requires a throughput quota increase.
cards.scope: per AWS Region.

cards.claim: AWS says that if an EFS file system on Bursting throughput is throughput-constrained, for example it uses more than 80% of the permitted throughput or has used all of its burst credits, you should use Elastic or Provisioned throughput instead.
cards.scope: EFS throughput modes.

cards.claim: AWS says to use Bursting throughput for EFS when you want throughput that scales with the amount of storage in your file system.
cards.scope: EFS throughput modes.

cards.claim: A file system can achieve a combined 100% of its read and write throughput.
cards.scope: per file system.

cards.claim: AWS recommends the default Elastic throughput mode for EFS when you have spiky or unpredictable workloads whose performance requirements are hard to forecast, or when your application drives throughput at an average-to-peak ratio of 5% or less.
cards.scope: EFS throughput modes.

cards.claim: AWS Transfer Family is a fully managed file transfer service for SFTP, FTPS and FTP; your end users can use their SFTP, FTP or FTPS clients to access data stored in your Amazon EFS file system, and Transfer Family endpoints must be in the same Region as the file system.
cards.scope: AWS Transfer Family with EFS.

cards.claim: Amazon EFS supports encryption in transit and encryption at rest; you enable encryption at rest when you create the file system, which encrypts all data and metadata, and you enable encryption in transit when you mount it.
cards.scope: Amazon EFS encryption.
links: [all of your data and metadata is encrypted](../facts/efs.md#efs-two-forms-encryption-when-enabled)

cards.claim: EFS One Zone file systems store data within a single Availability Zone. If all or part of that zone is lost or damaged, data stored in these file systems might be lost.
cards.scope: EFS One Zone file systems; loss or damage to all or part of the Availability Zone.

cards.claim: The AWS overview whitepaper names these EFS use cases: lift-and-shift enterprise applications, big data analytics, web serving and content management, application development and testing, media and entertainment workflows, database backups and container storage.
cards.scope: Amazon EFS.

cards.claim: Using Amazon EFS with Microsoft Windows-based Amazon EC2 instances is not supported.
cards.scope: Amazon EFS clients.

cards.claim: All write operations to files in IA or Archive are first written to Standard storage, and the data becomes eligible to transition again after 24 hours.
cards.scope: EFS lifecycle management.

cards.claim: The AWS case study says Adobe used Amazon FSx for Lustre high-performance file storage for fast access to data and to make sure GPU resources are never left idle.
cards.scope: customer case study on the AWS site; a customer statement published by AWS, not a service guarantee.

cards.claim: The AWS case study says Avionté uses Amazon FSx for Windows File Server, fully managed file storage built on Windows Server, to persist the application content of its remote desktop protocol based application.
cards.scope: customer case study on the AWS site; a customer statement published by AWS, not a service guarantee.

cards.claim: The AWS case study says Phillips 66 cycled 90 percent of its data into the elastic capacity-pool tier of FSx for NetApp ONTAP, which reduced its storage costs by 80 percent.
cards.scope: customer case study on the AWS site; a customer statement published by AWS, not a service guarantee.

cards.claim: The AWS case study says Phillips 66 migrated data center environments to Amazon EC2 and FSx for NetApp ONTAP, relied on NetApp SnapMirror for these migrations to preserve its existing data organization and security controls, and removed the need for code rewriting, rearchitecting or refactoring.
cards.scope: customer case study on the AWS site; a customer statement published by AWS, not a service guarantee.
links: [the need for code rewriting, rearchitecting, or refactoring](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-case-phillips66-snapmirror-no-refactoring)

cards.claim: On 2025-03-13 AWS Backup added logically air-gapped vault support for Amazon FSx for Lustre, Amazon FSx for Windows File Server and Amazon FSx for OpenZFS. A logically air-gapped vault stores immutable backup copies that are locked by default.
cards.scope: AWS Backup with Amazon FSx.

cards.claim: Amazon FSx File Gateway is listed in maintenance with an announcement date of 2024-10-28: it is no longer available to new customers, and existing customers can continue to use the service normally.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx File Gateway availability.

cards.claim: On 2024-11-27 FSx for Lustre began to let you create a Persistent 2 file system with Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) support for increased network performance; enabling EFA also provides support for GPUDirect Storage (GDS) and ENA Express.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre Persistent 2 file systems.

cards.claim: On 2025-05-29 FSx for Lustre added the Intelligent-Tiering storage class, which provides fully elastic storage with an optional SSD cache for low-latency access to frequently accessed data.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre storage classes.
links: [fully elastic storage with an optional SSD cache](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-change-lustre-intelligent-tiering-2025-05)

cards.claim: On 2024-06-06 FSx for Lustre began to let you create a Persistent 2 file system with a metadata configuration that provides the ability to increase metadata performance.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre Persistent 2 file systems.

cards.claim: On 2023-08-09 FSx for Lustre added release data repository tasks, which release archived files from a file system linked to an S3 data repository: releasing a file keeps the file listing and metadata but removes the local copy of the file content.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre linked to an S3 data repository.

cards.claim: On 2023-11-16 FSx for Lustre began to let you modify the throughput capacity of existing persistent SSD-based file systems as your throughput requirements evolve.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre persistent SSD-based file systems.

cards.claim: On 2025-02-12 FSx for Lustre began to let you upgrade the Lustre version of your file system to a newer version.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre.

cards.claim: On 2024-03-04 FSx for NetApp ONTAP added support for 12 HA pairs in scale-out file systems; file systems with 12 HA pairs can deliver up to 72 GBps of throughput capacity and 2,400,000 SSD IOPS.
cards.scope: FSx for NetApp ONTAP scale-out file systems.

cards.claim: On 2026-09-28 AWS Backup logically air-gapped vaults began to support Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP. A logically air-gapped vault stores immutable backups that are locked by default and isolated with encryption using AWS owned keys or customer-managed keys.
cards.scope: AWS Backup logically air-gapped vault with FSx for NetApp ONTAP.

cards.claim: On 2025-04-07 FSx for NetApp ONTAP began to support Autonomous Ransomware Protection (ARP), a NetApp AI-driven feature that monitors and protects against ransomware and malware attacks.
cards.scope: FSx for NetApp ONTAP security.

cards.claim: On 2025-08-14 FSx for NetApp ONTAP began to let you decrease the SSD storage capacity of second-generation file systems, to optimize storage costs for workloads with varying high-performance storage needs.
cards.scope: FSx for NetApp ONTAP second-generation SSD storage.

cards.claim: On 2024-07-09 FSx for NetApp ONTAP added support for the Non-Volatile Memory Express over TCP (NVMe/TCP) protocol.
cards.scope: FSx for NetApp ONTAP block protocols.

cards.claim: On 2025-12-02 FSx for NetApp ONTAP added Amazon S3 access points, a way to access data stored in FSx for ONTAP file systems with the Amazon S3 API without changing the existing file system configuration.
cards.scope: FSx for NetApp ONTAP file systems.

cards.claim: On 2024-07-09 FSx for NetApp ONTAP added second-generation Single-AZ and Multi-AZ file systems; a single high-availability (HA) pair now delivers up to 6 GBps of throughput capacity and 200,000 SSD IOPS.
cards.scope: FSx for NetApp ONTAP second-generation file systems.

cards.claim: On 2025-03-05 Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP eliminated SnapLock licensing fees for data stored in SnapLock volumes. The removal applies automatically to new and existing SnapLock volumes on all FSx for ONTAP file systems in all AWS Regions where they are available.
cards.scope: FSx for NetApp ONTAP SnapLock volumes.

cards.claim: On 2023-12-20 FSx for OpenZFS added cross-region and cross-account data replication.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS replication.

cards.claim: On 2024-12-01 FSx for OpenZFS added the Intelligent-Tiering storage class: fully elastic storage with an optional SSD cache, where you are billed for the data you store and do not need to specify a file system size at creation.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS storage classes.

cards.claim: On 2023-08-09 FSx for OpenZFS added the Multi-AZ deployment type.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS deployment types.

cards.claim: On 2026-05-13 FSx for OpenZFS began to let participant accounts create Multi-AZ file systems in VPCs shared with them in the same AWS organization. Before this, participant accounts could create Multi-AZ file systems only in VPCs they owned.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS Multi-AZ in shared VPCs.
cards.changed: 2026-05-13: was could only create Multi-AZ file systems in VPCs they owned

cards.claim: On 2023-11-26 FSx for OpenZFS added on-demand data replication.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS replication.

cards.claim: On 2025-06-25 FSx for OpenZFS added Amazon S3 access points attached to FSx for OpenZFS volumes, so you can use the S3 object API to access file data.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS volumes.

cards.claim: On 2024-07-09 FSx for OpenZFS added the Single-AZ (HA) deployment type.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS deployment types.

cards.claim: On 2025-11-19 FSx for Windows File Server added support for File Server Resource Manager (FSRM). FSRM support is available at no additional cost for new file systems in all AWS Regions where FSx for Windows File Server is available, and existing file systems get it during an upcoming maintenance window.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server FSRM.

cards.claim: On 2024-01-17 FSx for Windows File Server raised maximum IOPS from 350K to 400K for file systems with 12 GBps of throughput capacity or higher, and raised the maximum at lower throughput capacities as well.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server SSD IOPS, 12 GBps throughput capacity.

cards.claim: On 2023-08-09 FSx for Windows File Server file systems began to support up to 12 GBps throughput capacity.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server throughput capacity.

cards.claim: On 2023-08-09 FSx for Windows File Server file systems began to support SSD IOPS provisioning independently of storage capacity.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server SSD IOPS.

cards.claim: On 2023-08-09 FSx for Windows File Server file systems began to support updating the storage type from HDD to SSD.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server storage type.

cards.claim: On the AWS page comparing FSx file systems, access control lists are marked for FSx for NetApp ONTAP (NFS 4.0, v4.1, NTFS) and FSx for Windows File Server (NTFS), and not for OpenZFS or Lustre.
cards.scope: security and compliance table.

cards.claim: On the AWS page comparing FSx file systems, Active Directory support for file system access authentication and access control is marked only for FSx for NetApp ONTAP and FSx for Windows File Server.
cards.scope: security and compliance table.
links: [Active Directory support for file system access authentication](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-compare-active-directory-ontap-windows)

cards.claim: On the AWS page comparing FSx file systems, anti-virus integration is marked only for FSx for NetApp ONTAP.
cards.scope: security and compliance table.

cards.claim: AWS lists the availability SLA as 99.99% for Multi-AZ and 99.9% for Single-AZ on FSx for NetApp ONTAP; 99.99% for Multi-AZ and 99.5% for Single-AZ on OpenZFS and Windows File Server; and 99.5% for Single-AZ on Lustre.
cards.scope: per FSx file system type and deployment type.

cards.claim: AWS lists client compatibility as Windows, Linux and macOS for FSx for NetApp ONTAP, OpenZFS and Windows File Server, and Linux for FSx for Lustre.
cards.scope: per FSx file system type.

cards.claim: For cost-optimized storage of cold, infrequently accessed data, AWS lists a low-cost tier with cold data cycled to it automatically for FSx for NetApp ONTAP, an HDD storage option for FSx for Windows File Server and an HDD storage option for FSx for Lustre; FSx for OpenZFS is not marked.
