cards.scope: price/performance table, FSx file system comparison page.

cards.claim: AWS lists the same compliance programs for all four FSx file system types, among them HIPAA BAA, PCI/DSS, ISO, SOC, IRAP, GDPR, ISMAP, FINMA, MTCS, C5, ENS High, OSPAR and HITRUST CSF.
cards.scope: security and compliance table.

cards.claim: On the AWS page comparing FSx file systems, cross-Region replication is marked for FSx for NetApp ONTAP (NetApp SnapMirror) and for FSx for Lustre (using S3 cross-region replication), and not for OpenZFS or Windows File Server.
cards.scope: availability and data protection table.

cards.claim: On the AWS page comparing FSx file systems, data deduplication is marked only for FSx for NetApp ONTAP and FSx for Windows File Server, and it applies to both file system storage and backups.
cards.scope: price/performance table, FSx file system comparison page.

cards.claim: AWS lists deployment options of Single-AZ and Multi-AZ for FSx for NetApp ONTAP, OpenZFS and Windows File Server, and Single-AZ with Persistent or Scratch for FSx for Lustre.
cards.scope: per FSx file system type.

cards.claim: On the AWS page comparing FSx file systems, file access auditing is marked only for FSx for NetApp ONTAP and FSx for Windows File Server.
cards.scope: security and compliance table.

cards.claim: On the AWS page comparing FSx file systems, instant cloning is marked only for FSx for NetApp ONTAP and FSx for OpenZFS.
cards.scope: availability and data protection table.

cards.claim: AWS lists latency of less than 1 ms for FSx for NetApp ONTAP, FSx for Windows File Server and FSx for Lustre, and less than 0.5 ms for FSx for OpenZFS.
cards.scope: per FSx file system type.

cards.claim: On the AWS page comparing FSx file systems, only FSx for Lustre is marked as supporting automatic import and export of S3 data sets.
cards.scope: FSx file system comparison page.

cards.claim: AWS lists maximum file system size as virtually unlimited (tens of PBs) for FSx for NetApp ONTAP, 512 TiB for OpenZFS, 64 TiB for Windows File Server and multiple PBs for Lustre.
cards.scope: per file system, per FSx file system type; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: AWS lists maximum IOPS per file system as millions for FSx for NetApp ONTAP, 1-2 million for OpenZFS, hundreds of thousands for Windows File Server and millions for Lustre.
cards.scope: per file system, per FSx file system type; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: AWS lists maximum throughput per file system of 72-80 GB/s for FSx for NetApp ONTAP, 10-21 GB/s for OpenZFS, 12-20 GB/s for Windows File Server and 1000 GB/s for Lustre. The lower number of a range is baseline throughput, and the upper number is a higher level enabled by caching, bursting and compression.
cards.scope: per file system, per FSx file system type; maximum; not adjustable; a range gives baseline (lower) to enhanced (upper) throughput.

cards.claim: AWS lists maximum throughput available to a single client accessing a file system as 18 GB/s for FSx for NetApp ONTAP, 10 GB/s for OpenZFS, 20 GB/s for Windows File Server and 150 GB/s for Lustre.
cards.scope: per client, per FSx file system type; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: On the AWS page comparing FSx file systems, only FSx for NetApp ONTAP is marked for compute burst to the cloud, using FSx as an on-AWS cache of on-premises data with NetApp FlexCache.
cards.scope: hybrid usage, FSx file system comparison page.

cards.claim: On the AWS page comparing FSx file systems, only FSx for NetApp ONTAP is marked for on-premises caching of FSx data, with NetApp Global File Cache and NetApp FlexCache.
cards.scope: hybrid usage, FSx file system comparison page.

cards.claim: On the AWS page comparing FSx file systems, only FSx for NetApp ONTAP is marked for backup and disaster recovery from on premises to AWS, using NetApp SnapMirror.
cards.scope: hybrid usage, FSx file system comparison page.

cards.claim: AWS lists protocol support as SMB, NFS and iSCSI for FSx for NetApp ONTAP, NFS for OpenZFS, SMB for Windows File Server, and a custom POSIX-compliant protocol optimized for performance for Lustre.
cards.scope: per FSx file system type.

cards.claim: On the AWS page comparing FSx file systems, inline instantaneous snapshots are marked for FSx for NetApp ONTAP, OpenZFS and Windows File Server, and are not marked for FSx for Lustre.
cards.scope: availability and data protection table.

cards.claim: In the AWS storage decision guide table, the cache storage type is served by Amazon File Cache, a fully managed, scalable, high-speed cache on AWS for processing file data stored in disparate locations, including on-premises NFS file systems, cloud file systems (FSx for OpenZFS, FSx for NetApp ONTAP) and Amazon S3.
cards.scope: storage type table of the decision guide.

cards.claim: The AWS storage decision guide says the Amazon FSx data storage family comes in four options that align to popular file systems: Windows File Server, Lustre, OpenZFS and NetApp ONTAP.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx family.
links: [four options that align to popular file systems](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-decision-guide-four-file-systems-align-to-popular)

cards.claim: The AWS storage decision guide says FSx for Lustre is optimized for workloads where speed matters, such as machine learning, high performance computing (HPC), video processing and financial modeling.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for Lustre.

cards.claim: In the AWS storage decision guide, the online migration options include AWS DataSync, AWS Transfer Family, Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP SnapMirror and AWS Storage Gateway, and online migration is optimized for frequent updates to data and for time-critical or ongoing workloads.
cards.scope: migration options table of the decision guide.
links: [Online is optimized for frequent updates to data](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-decision-guide-online-migration-options)

cards.claim: The AWS storage decision guide says that if you already use NetApp ONTAP appliances on premises, Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP gives a seamless migration path.
cards.scope: migration compatibility criterion in the storage decision guide.

cards.claim: The AWS storage decision guide says Windows-based clients can use Amazon FSx for Windows File Server, which gives highly available storage with full SMB support, and that FSx for Lustre is designed for Unix and Linux based file systems.
cards.scope: client type criterion in the storage decision guide.

cards.claim: Amazon FSx for Lustre always encrypts your file system data and your backups at rest using keys you manage through AWS KMS.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre encryption at rest.

cards.claim: Amazon FSx stores backups with 99.999999999% (11 9's) of durability on Amazon S3.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre backups; fixed.

cards.claim: Amazon FSx takes daily automatic backups of FSx for Lustre file systems and allows additional backups at any point; backups are incremental.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre backups.

cards.claim: Backups are not supported on FSx for Lustre file systems linked to an S3 bucket, because the S3 bucket serves as the primary storage location for the full dataset.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre linked to Amazon S3.

cards.claim: Backups are not supported on FSx for Lustre scratch file systems because they are designed for temporary storage and shorter-term processing of data.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre scratch file systems.

cards.claim: FSx for Lustre provides consistent, sub-millisecond latencies for file operations.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre file operations.

cards.claim: You link a file system to S3 buckets by creating data repository associations using the Amazon FSx console, the AWS CLI, or the Amazon FSx API.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre with Amazon S3.

cards.claim: Amazon FSx for Lustre provides two deployment options: scratch and persistent.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre deployment options.

cards.claim: FSx for Lustre with EFA support enabled provides up to 7x, or up to 700 Gbps, higher per-client throughput compared with previous FSx for Lustre file systems.
cards.scope: per client, EFA-enabled FSx for Lustre; maximum.

cards.claim: Intelligent-Tiering provides up to 34% lower costs compared with traditional on-premises HDD deployments.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre Intelligent-Tiering; maximum.

cards.claim: The Intelligent-Tiering storage class provides fully elastic, intelligently tiered storage with an optional SSD read cache to speed up access to frequently accessed data.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre Intelligent-Tiering storage class.

cards.claim: With Intelligent-Tiering, data in the SSD read cache has sub-millisecond time-to-first-byte latencies, and all other data has time-to-first-byte latencies in the range of tens of milliseconds.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre Intelligent-Tiering.

cards.claim: Intelligent-Tiering file systems can be provisioned with multiples of 4,000 MB/s of throughput capacity, independent of storage capacity.
cards.scope: per file system, Intelligent-Tiering; fixed; not adjustable.

cards.claim: FSx for Lustre data compression uses the LZ4 algorithm, which is optimized for compression speed, so enabling compression will not adversely impact file system performance.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre data compression.

cards.claim: When metadata IOPS are increased, FSx automatically adds a new metadata server for each 12,000 metadata IOPS provisioned.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre metadata servers.

cards.claim: You can create multiple FSx for Lustre file systems linked to the same S3 bucket.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre linked to Amazon S3.

cards.claim: FSx will not take automatic backups of an FSx for Lustre file system if it is linked to S3.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre linked to Amazon S3.

cards.claim: On a persistent file system, if a file server becomes unavailable it is replaced automatically and within minutes.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre persistent file systems.

cards.claim: You can release inactive data from S3-linked FSx for Lustre file systems by using a data repository task.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre linked to Amazon S3.

cards.claim: Releasing file system data does not ensure that an FSx for Lustre file system will never become full.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre linked to Amazon S3.

cards.claim: Instead of automatic import and export, you can import and export batches of new and changed data between the file system and S3 for fine-grained control over data synchronization.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre linked to Amazon S3.

cards.claim: You can link an FSx for Lustre file system to S3 buckets, and FSx for Lustre makes the S3 data transparently accessible in the file system.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre with Amazon S3.
links: [link your Amazon FSx for Lustre file system](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-faq-lustre-s3-link-transparent)

cards.claim: The content of an S3 object is imported automatically only when you first access the associated file on the file system, so an object's data does not consume file system space unless accessed at least once.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre linked to Amazon S3.
links: [imported automatically from S3 only when you access](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-faq-lustre-s3-object-imported-on-first-access)

cards.claim: FSx for Lustre can be configured to keep content synchronized in both directions between the file system and the linked S3 buckets.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre linked to Amazon S3.

cards.claim: The SSD storage class is provisioned: you specify a file system size and pay storage costs for the amount of storage provisioned.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre SSD storage class.

cards.claim: Amazon FSx for Lustre offers SSD and Intelligent-Tiering storage classes.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre storage classes.

cards.claim: You can increase an FSx for Lustre file system's storage capacity every six hours, in the same increments that you can provision new file systems.
cards.scope: per file system, storage capacity increase; fixed; not adjustable.

cards.claim: FSx for Lustre file systems scale to TB/s of throughput and millions of IOPS.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre.

cards.claim: SSD-based FSx for Lustre file systems can be provisioned with 125, 250, 500, or 1,000 MB/s of throughput per TiB of storage provisioned.
cards.scope: per TiB of storage provisioned, SSD-based file systems; fixed; not adjustable.

cards.claim: You are required to unmount all clients from an FSx for Lustre file system before initiating a Lustre version upgrade.
cards.scope: FSx for Lustre version upgrades.

cards.claim: Each gigabyte of FSx for NetApp ONTAP SSD storage includes 3 disk IOPS, and additional IOPS can be provisioned as needed.
cards.scope: per GB of SSD storage; default; adjustable.

cards.claim: You can optionally join an FSx for ONTAP file system to your organization's Active Directory so users can use their existing AD-based identities to authenticate and access it over NFS or SMB.
cards.scope: FSx for NetApp ONTAP authentication.
links: [join your file system to your organization’s AD](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-faq-ontap-active-directory-nfs-smb)

cards.claim: As you write data to FSx for ONTAP, less frequently accessed data is automatically transitioned to the capacity pool tier, which grows and shrinks with the amount of data tiered to it.
cards.scope: FSx for NetApp ONTAP capacity pool tiering.

cards.claim: FSx for ONTAP backups are a crash-consistent and secondary, offline copy of a volume in your file system.
cards.scope: FSx for NetApp ONTAP backups.
links: [crash-consistent and secondary, offline copy of a volume](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-faq-ontap-backups-crash-consistent-offline)

cards.claim: By default, Amazon FSx takes an automatic backup of your FSx for ONTAP volumes each day during a backup window that you specify.
cards.scope: FSx for NetApp ONTAP volumes; default; adjustable.

cards.claim: Backups for both Multi-AZ and Single-AZ FSx for ONTAP file systems are stored across multiple AZs to achieve high durability.
cards.scope: FSx for NetApp ONTAP backups.

cards.claim: Capacity pool storage is a fully elastic storage tier that can scale to petabytes in size and is cost-optimized for infrequently accessed data.
cards.scope: FSx for NetApp ONTAP capacity pool storage.

cards.claim: You do not need to provision storage for data in an FSx for ONTAP file system's capacity pool.
cards.scope: FSx for NetApp ONTAP capacity pool storage.

cards.claim: You can access FSx for NetApp ONTAP data from Linux, Windows, or macOS instances running on Amazon EC2, ECS, EKS, VMware Cloud on AWS, Red Hat OpenShift Service on AWS, Amazon WorkSpaces, and Amazon AppStream 2.0.
cards.scope: FSx for NetApp ONTAP clients.

cards.claim: You can enable compression and deduplication for data in SSD storage, and the savings are preserved when data is tiered to capacity pool storage. Storage efficiency is always enabled for backup data.

cards.claim: The default for ONTAP file systems is 100, the maximum number of Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP file systems that you can create in this account.
cards.scope: per account, per AWS Region; default; adjustable.

cards.claim: The default for ONTAP SSD storage capacity is 524,288, the maximum amount of SSD storage capacity (in GiB) for all Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP file systems that you can have in this account.
cards.scope: per account, per AWS Region, all ONTAP file systems; default; adjustable.

cards.claim: The default for ONTAP SSD IOPS is 1,000,000, the maximum amount of SSD IOPS for all Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP file systems that you can have in this account.
cards.scope: per account, per AWS Region, all ONTAP file systems; default; adjustable.

cards.claim: The default for ONTAP throughput capacity is 10,240, the maximum amount of throughput capacity (in MBps) for all Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP file systems that you can have in this account.
cards.scope: per account, per AWS Region, all ONTAP file systems; default; adjustable.

cards.claim: You can restore an FSx for ONTAP volume backup to any existing FSx for ONTAP file system you have access to that is in the same AWS Region where the backup is stored.
cards.scope: FSx for ONTAP backups.
links: [same AWS Region where the backup is stored](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-ontap-restore-backup-same-region-copy-first-for-other-region)

cards.claim: Amazon S3 enforces Block public access by default for all access points attached to an FSx for ONTAP volume, and you cannot modify or disable this setting.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP S3 access points.

cards.claim: An S3 access point attached to an FSx for ONTAP volume lets you access file data through the S3 API while the data stays on the file system and you keep using NFS and SMB alongside it.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP S3 access points.
links: [access your file data using the S3 API](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-ontap-s3-access-points-s3-api-on-file-data-no-copy)

cards.claim: Single-AZ 1 is a first-generation file system with one high-availability pair, whereas Single-AZ 2 is a second-generation file system with 1 to 12 HA pairs.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP Single-AZ.

cards.claim: A Single-AZ FSx for ONTAP file system provisions one to twelve pairs of active-standby file servers, with the active and standby server of each pair in separate fault domains within one Availability Zone.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP Single-AZ.
links: [separate fault domains within a single Availability Zone](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-ontap-single-az-active-standby-pairs-separate-fault-domains)

cards.claim: During planned maintenance or an unplanned disruption of an active file server, Amazon FSx automatically and independently fails over that HA pair to the standby file server, typically within a few seconds, with no manual intervention.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP Single-AZ.

cards.claim: Single-AZ FSx for ONTAP file systems suit use cases that do not require the data resiliency of Multi-AZ, such as development and test environments or secondary copies of data already stored on premises or in other Regions, because they replicate data only within a single Availability Zone.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP Single-AZ.
links: [only replicating data within a single Availability Zone](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-ontap-single-az-for-dev-test-secondary-copies)

cards.claim: On Single-AZ FSx for ONTAP file systems the NFS, SMB and management endpoints are secondary IP addresses within the VPC's CIDR range, so clients can use VPC Peering, Direct Connect or Site-to-Site VPN without AWS Transit Gateway.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP Single-AZ.

cards.claim: After a file is moved to the WORM state on a SnapLock Compliance volume, no user can delete it before its retention period expires.
cards.scope: FSx for ONTAP SnapLock Compliance.
links: [can't be deleted before its retention period expires](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-ontap-snaplock-compliance-no-delete-by-any-user)

cards.claim: You can use SnapLock Compliance to address government or industry-specific mandates such as SEC Rule 17a-4(f), FINRA Rule 4511 and CFTC Regulation 1.31.
cards.scope: FSx for ONTAP SnapLock Compliance.

cards.claim: SnapLock Enterprise lets you authorize only specific users to delete files, and you can use it to test retention settings before using SnapLock Compliance.
cards.scope: FSx for ONTAP SnapLock Enterprise.

cards.claim: You must decide at volume creation whether a volume uses SnapLock, a non-SnapLock volume can't be converted to a SnapLock volume, and a SnapLock volume can't be converted between Enterprise and Compliance.
cards.scope: FSx for ONTAP SnapLock.

cards.claim: SnapLock moves files to a write once, read many (WORM) state that prevents modification or deletion for a specified retention period, and FSx for ONTAP supports the Compliance and Enterprise retention modes.
cards.scope: FSx for ONTAP SnapLock.

cards.claim: AWS recommends using NetApp SnapMirror to migrate on-premises NetApp ONTAP file systems to FSx for ONTAP.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP migration.

cards.claim: You can use NetApp SnapMirror to schedule periodic replication of an FSx for ONTAP file system to or from a second file system, in-Region or cross-Region, as frequently as every 5 minutes.
cards.scope: FSx for ONTAP SnapMirror.

cards.claim: Only volume-level SnapMirror replication is supported by FSx for ONTAP, and synchronous SnapMirror, including StrictSync, is not supported.
cards.scope: FSx for ONTAP SnapMirror.

cards.claim: You can store a maximum of 1,023 snapshots per volume at any point in time.
cards.scope: per FSx for ONTAP volume; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: With ONTAP snapshots, users can view and restore individual files or folders from an earlier snapshot to undo changes, recover deleted content and compare file versions.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP snapshots.

cards.claim: You can increase the SSD storage capacity of an FSx for ONTAP file system as your storage needs grow, and on second-generation file systems you can also decrease SSD storage capacity.
cards.scope: FSx for NetApp ONTAP SSD storage.

cards.claim: The typical storage capacity savings for general purpose file sharing workloads is 65% from compression, deduplication and compaction on both the SSD and capacity pool tiers, without sacrificing performance.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP storage efficiency.

cards.claim: FSx for ONTAP supports access over NFS (v3, v4.0, v4.1 and v4.2), all versions of SMB (including 2.0, 3.0 and 3.1.1) and the iSCSI protocol.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP clients.

cards.claim: A storage virtual machine (SVM) is an isolated file server with its own administrative and data access endpoints, and you can join SVMs to a Microsoft Active Directory for file access authentication and authorization.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP SVM.

cards.claim: You can test failover on an FSx for ONTAP file system by modifying its throughput capacity.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP failover.

cards.claim: Data is tiered 24 to 48 hours after its cooling period expires, and tiering is a background process with a lower priority than client-facing requests.
cards.scope: FSx for ONTAP volume tiering.

cards.claim: The All tiering policy marks all user data and snapshot data as cold and stores it in the capacity pool tier, where data blocks stay cold when read; file metadata always remains on the SSD tier.
cards.scope: FSx for ONTAP volume tiering policy All.
links: [file metadata always remains on the SSD tier](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-ontap-tiering-policy-all-marks-everything-cold)

cards.claim: The Auto tiering policy moves all cold user data and snapshots to the capacity pool tier; the cooling period is 31 days by default and configurable from 2 to 183 days, and Auto is the default policy when creating a volume in the console.
cards.scope: FSx for ONTAP volume tiering policy Auto; default; adjustable.

cards.claim: The None tiering policy keeps all of a volume's data on the primary storage tier and prevents it from being moved to capacity pool storage.
cards.scope: FSx for ONTAP volume tiering policy None.

cards.claim: Data tiering automatically moves data between the SSD and capacity pool tiers; each volume has a tiering policy that controls whether cold data moves to the capacity tier, and the cooling period determines when data becomes cold.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP storage tiers.
links: [tiering policy that controls whether data is moved](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-ontap-tiering-policy-per-volume-cooling-period)

cards.claim: The Snapshot Only tiering policy moves only snapshot data to the capacity pool tier, with a cooling period that is 2 days by default and configurable from 2 to 183 days; it is the default policy when creating a volume with the AWS CLI, API or ONTAP CLI.
cards.scope: FSx for ONTAP volume tiering policy Snapshot Only; default; adjustable.

cards.claim: An FSx for ONTAP file system has two storage tiers: primary storage, which is provisioned high-performance SSD storage for the active portion of your data, and capacity pool storage, which is fully elastic, scales to petabytes and is cost optimized for infrequently accessed data.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP storage tiers.

cards.claim: User-initiated FSx for ONTAP backups are retained forever unless you delete them, and they are retained even after you delete the volume or the file system.
cards.scope: FSx for ONTAP backups.

cards.claim: You can use FSx for ONTAP as an external datastore for VMware Cloud on AWS Software-Defined Data Centers (SDDCs).
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP.

cards.claim: FSx for ONTAP volumes are logical containers hosted on SVMs, and they are thin provisioned, so they only consume storage capacity for the data stored in them.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP volumes.

cards.claim: AWS says that for customers who use NetApp ONTAP on premises, FSx for ONTAP is an ideal solution to migrate, back up or burst file-based applications to AWS without changing the application code or how they manage their data.
cards.scope: FSx for NetApp ONTAP.
links: [migrate, back up, or burst your file-based applications](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-ontap-what-is-migrate-backup-burst-from-on-premises-ontap)

cards.claim: FSx for ONTAP offers multi-protocol access to data using the NFS, SMB, iSCSI and NVMe protocols, and its file storage is broadly accessible from Linux, Windows and macOS compute instances running in AWS or on premises.
cards.scope: FSx for NetApp ONTAP.

cards.claim: AWS says that with FSx for ONTAP you can achieve SSD levels of performance for your workload while paying for SSD storage for only a small fraction of your data; in addition, FSx for ONTAP automatically tiers your data to lower-cost, elastic storage.
cards.scope: FSx for NetApp ONTAP.

cards.claim: Amazon FSx provides access control for OpenZFS at the file system level with VPC security groups, at the API level with IAM access policies, and at the file and folder level with Unix permissions.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for OpenZFS.

cards.claim: By default Amazon FSx takes an automatic daily backup of an FSx for OpenZFS file system; the console default retention is 30 days, the maximum retention for automatic backups is 90 days, and user-initiated backups are kept forever unless you delete them.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS backups; default; adjustable.
links: [default automatic daily backup retention period is 30 days](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-openzfs-automatic-daily-backup-default-30-days-console-user-kept-forever)

cards.claim: FSx for OpenZFS backups are file-system-consistent, highly durable and incremental, and Amazon FSx stores them in Amazon S3.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS backups.

cards.claim: For in-AWS applications, AWS recommends launching clients in the same Availability Zone as the preferred file server to minimize latency.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS.
links: [same Availability Zone as your preferred file server](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-openzfs-clients-same-az-as-preferred-file-server)

cards.claim: A clone volume is a writable copy initialized with the same data as the snapshot, created almost instantly and initially consuming no additional storage; it keeps a dependency on its source snapshot, so you cannot delete the snapshot while the clone is in use.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS clones.

cards.claim: FSx for OpenZFS volumes support Zstandard compression, which gives very high on-disk compression with higher read throughput and reduced write throughput than LZ4, and LZ4 compression, which gives higher write throughput but lower compression than Zstandard.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS data compression.

cards.claim: Amazon FSx automatically encrypts FSx for OpenZFS data at rest in file systems and backups using keys that you manage in AWS KMS.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for OpenZFS encryption.

cards.claim: An FSx for OpenZFS failover typically takes less than 60 seconds from failure detection to promotion of the standby, the file system automatically fails back to the recovered preferred file server usually in less than 60 seconds, and I/O might be briefly paused during failover and failback.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS failover.

cards.claim: Multi-AZ (HA) and Single-AZ (HA) file systems automatically fail over to the standby file server when the preferred file server becomes unavailable, when the throughput capacity is changed, or when it undergoes planned maintenance, and Multi-AZ (HA) file systems also fail over if an Availability Zone disruption occurs.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS failover.

cards.claim: A full-copy volume is a fully independent writable copy of a snapshot, but because all of the data must be transferred it can take significantly longer to create than a clone volume.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS clones.

cards.claim: Amazon FSx for OpenZFS is a fully managed file storage service that makes it easy to move data to AWS from on-premises ZFS or other Linux-based file servers.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for OpenZFS.

cards.claim: FSx for OpenZFS file systems that use the Intelligent-Tiering storage class use fully elastic, intelligently tiered, regional block storage that automatically grows and shrinks to fit the workload.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS Intelligent-Tiering storage class.

cards.claim: Data access from Intelligent-Tiering storage has time-to-first-byte latencies of roughly tens of milliseconds and per-request costs, while accesses from the SSD read cache return with sub-millisecond latency and no per-request costs.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS Intelligent-Tiering storage class.

cards.claim: With the Intelligent-Tiering storage class you do not need to provision IOPS; you pay for data access based on usage, in the form of read and write requests.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS Intelligent-Tiering storage class.

cards.claim: You can configure the SSD read cache of an Intelligent-Tiering file system with one of three sizing modes, Automatic, Custom or None.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS Intelligent-Tiering storage class.

cards.claim: The maximum retention period for automated backups of an FSx for OpenZFS file system is 90 days.
cards.scope: per file system; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: The maximum storage capacity for FSx for OpenZFS file systems using the Intelligent-Tiering storage class is 512 TiB.
cards.scope: per file system, Intelligent-Tiering; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: The maximum storage capacity for FSx for OpenZFS Single-AZ 2 (non-HA and HA) file systems is 512 TiB.
cards.scope: per Single-AZ 2 (non-HA and HA) file system; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: The maximum number of snapshots per FSx for OpenZFS file system is 700.
cards.scope: per file system; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: The maximum throughput capacity of an FSx for OpenZFS file system is 10,240 MBps.
cards.scope: per file system; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: The maximum number of volumes per FSx for OpenZFS file system is 100.
cards.scope: per file system; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: The minimum storage capacity of an FSx for OpenZFS file system is 64 GiB.
cards.scope: per file system; minimum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: The minimum throughput capacity of an FSx for OpenZFS file system is 64 MBps.
cards.scope: per file system; minimum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: The maximum number of tags per FSx for OpenZFS file system is 50.
cards.scope: per file system; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: The maximum retention period for user-initiated backups of an FSx for OpenZFS file system is no retention limit.
cards.scope: per file system; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: The maximum number of user and group quotas per FSx for OpenZFS volume is 100.
cards.scope: per volume; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: You can migrate between FSx for OpenZFS deployment types by restoring from a backup, by using rsync, or by using on-demand replication.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS deployment types.

cards.claim: Multi-AZ (HA) file systems replicate data and support failover across multiple Availability Zones in the same Region, with a separate copy of the data in each Availability Zone, and failover typically completes within 60 seconds.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS Multi-AZ (HA).

cards.claim: Multi-AZ (HA) file systems are recommended for business-critical production workloads and database workloads that need storage that is highly available and durable across Availability Zones in the same Region.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS Multi-AZ (HA).

cards.claim: FSx for OpenZFS Multi-AZ (HA) file systems replicate data synchronously within each Availability Zone and between the two Availability Zones, and fail over to the standby Availability Zone automatically, typically within 60 seconds.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS Multi-AZ (HA) deployment.

cards.claim: Amazon FSx for OpenZFS file systems are accessible from Linux, Windows and macOS compute instances and containers using the NFS protocol (v3, v4.0, v4.1, v4.2).
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for OpenZFS.

cards.claim: FSx for OpenZFS supports on-demand data replication, which transfers snapshots of data between file systems within and across AWS Regions and accounts, and it is available for all deployment types in Regions where FSx for OpenZFS is available.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS replication.

cards.claim: With ongoing periodic data replication you can schedule an automatic snapshot of a source volume and an incremental replication of that snapshot to a destination volume at a certain interval, for example every 15 minutes.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS replication.
links: [automatically takes a snapshot of a source volume](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-openzfs-periodic-replication-schedule-incremental)

cards.claim: For FSx for OpenZFS Multi-AZ file systems there are no data transfer fees and cross-AZ data replication costs are included in the throughput capacity price. For Single-AZ file systems you pay for data transfer in both directions when you access the file system from a non-preferred Availability Zone in the same Region.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS data transfer.

cards.claim: For FSx for OpenZFS, pricing is quoted on a monthly basis, usage is prorated by the second, and you are billed for your average usage over a month.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS.

cards.claim: For FSx for OpenZFS, 3 IOPS are included for every GB of SSD storage by default.
cards.scope: per GB of SSD storage; default.

cards.claim: The default for OpenZFS backups is 10,000, the maximum number of user-initiated backups for all Amazon FSx for OpenZFS file systems that you can have in this account.
cards.scope: per account, per AWS Region, all OpenZFS file systems; default; adjustable.

cards.claim: The default for OpenZFS disk IOPS is 400,000, the total amount of disk IOPS allowed for all Amazon FSx for OpenZFS file systems in this account.
cards.scope: per account, per AWS Region, all OpenZFS file systems; default; adjustable.

cards.claim: The default for OpenZFS file systems is 100, the maximum number of Amazon FSx for OpenZFS file systems that you can create in this account.
cards.scope: per account, per AWS Region; default; adjustable.

cards.claim: The default for OpenZFS SSD storage capacity is 65,536 (262,144 in US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), and US West (Oregon)), the maximum amount of SSD storage capacity (in GiB) that you can configure for all Amazon FSx for OpenZFS file systems in this account.
cards.scope: per account, per AWS Region, all OpenZFS file systems; default; adjustable.

cards.claim: The default for OpenZFS throughput capacity is 10,240, the total amount of throughput capacity (in MBps) allowed for all Amazon FSx for OpenZFS file systems in this account.
cards.scope: per account, per AWS Region, all OpenZFS file systems; default; adjustable.

cards.claim: When you create a volume, the default ZFS record size for FSx for OpenZFS file systems using the Intelligent-Tiering storage class is 1024 KiB.
cards.scope: per volume, Intelligent-Tiering storage class; default; adjustable.

cards.claim: When you create an FSx for OpenZFS volume, the default ZFS record size is 128 KiB for file systems that do not use the Intelligent-Tiering storage class (Intelligent-Tiering file systems default to 1024 KiB).
cards.scope: per volume, file systems that do not use Intelligent-Tiering; default; adjustable.

cards.claim: On-demand data replication can synchronize data to development or test environments, maintain read replicas for scale-out read performance, and maintain a passive standby file system for disaster recovery.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS replication.

cards.claim: S3 access points are named network endpoints that attach to either S3 general purpose buckets or FSx for OpenZFS volumes, so applications that work with S3 can use file data on FSx for OpenZFS without changes or moving data out of file storage.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for OpenZFS S3 access points.

cards.claim: Amazon S3 access points for FSx for OpenZFS file systems deliver latency in the tens of milliseconds range, consistent with S3 bucket access.
cards.scope: S3 access points for FSx for OpenZFS.

cards.claim: FSx for OpenZFS provides OpenZFS data management capabilities including data compression, near instant point-in-time snapshots and data cloning, designed for use with the Amazon FSx API.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for OpenZFS.

cards.claim: Single-AZ 2 file systems offer double the performance scalability of Single-AZ 1, delivering up to 400,000 IOPS and 10 GBps throughput for both reads and writes to persistent SSD storage.
cards.scope: per FSx for OpenZFS Single-AZ 2 file system, persistent SSD storage; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: FSx for OpenZFS Single-AZ 2 file systems include an up to 2.5 TB high-speed NVMe read cache that caches your most recently-accessed data, making that data accessible at millions of IOPS and with latencies of a few hundred microseconds.
cards.scope: per FSx for OpenZFS Single-AZ 2 file system; maximum.

cards.claim: For all Single-AZ file systems, file system failure may be unrecoverable in rare cases, such as storage component failures, and then you recover the file system from the most recent backup.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS Single-AZ.

cards.claim: FSx for OpenZFS Single-AZ (HA) file systems fail over from the primary file server to the standby file server typically within 60 seconds during planned maintenance events or unplanned service disruptions.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS Single-AZ (HA) file systems.

cards.claim: Single-AZ (HA) file systems deploy a primary and a standby file system within the same Availability Zone to give continuous availability during failover and failback, and failover typically completes within 60 seconds.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS Single-AZ (HA).

cards.claim: Single-AZ (HA) file systems are recommended as a cost-effective solution for workloads that need high availability but not storage redundancy across Availability Zones, including analytics and EDA workloads.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS Single-AZ (HA).
links: [cost-effective solution for workloads that need high availability](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-openzfs-single-az-ha-recommended-analytics-eda)

cards.claim: Single-AZ (non-HA) file systems usually experience about 30 minutes of downtime during failure recovery and the planned maintenance window, and suit workloads that can tolerate temporary loss of availability and, in rare cases, the loss of data updates since the most recent backup.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS Single-AZ (non-HA).

cards.claim: Single-AZ (non-HA) file systems recover by themselves within a single Availability Zone by detecting and addressing component failures automatically, and recovery typically completes within 30 minutes.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS Single-AZ (non-HA).

cards.claim: A snapshot is a read-only image of an FSx for OpenZFS volume at a point in time, and with snapshots users can view and restore individual folders and files from an earlier snapshot.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS snapshots.
links: [read-only image of an FSx for OpenZFS volume](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-openzfs-snapshot-read-only-image-restore-files)

cards.claim: The recommendation is to keep storage utilization of SSD (provisioned) FSx for OpenZFS file systems below 80% of the total capacity.
cards.scope: per SSD (provisioned) file system; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: FSx for OpenZFS supports three file system deployment types, Multi-AZ (HA), Single-AZ (HA) and Single-AZ (non-HA), each with a different level of availability and durability.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for OpenZFS.

cards.claim: FSx for OpenZFS has two storage classes: Intelligent-Tiering, where you are billed for the data you store and do not specify a file system size, and SSD, where you specify a file system size and pay for the storage you provision.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS storage classes.

cards.claim: FSx for OpenZFS supports multiple volumes per file system, thin provisioning, and user and group quotas for cost-efficient shared file systems across multiple users and applications.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for OpenZFS.

cards.claim: FSx for OpenZFS file systems are accessible from Linux, Windows and macOS compute instances and containers through the industry-standard NFS protocol, and support OpenZFS features such as instant point-in-time snapshots and data cloning.
cards.scope: FSx for OpenZFS.

cards.claim: The AWS overview whitepaper says FSx for Lustre is seamlessly integrated with Amazon S3, so you can link long-term data sets with high-performance file systems for compute-intensive workloads.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for Lustre.

cards.claim: The AWS overview whitepaper says FSx for NetApp ONTAP offers high-performance file storage accessible from Linux, Windows and macOS compute instances through the NFS, SMB and iSCSI protocols.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP.

cards.claim: The AWS overview whitepaper says FSx for OpenZFS makes it easy to migrate on-premises file servers without changing your applications or how you manage data.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for OpenZFS.

cards.claim: The AWS overview whitepaper says FSx for Windows File Server is built on Windows Server and supports the SMB protocol and Windows NTFS, Active Directory integration and Distributed File System (DFS).
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server.

cards.claim: The AWS page on choosing an FSx file system recommends FSx for Lustre when your current storage technology is Lustre or another parallel file system.
cards.scope: FSx file system choice by current storage technology.

cards.claim: The AWS page on choosing an FSx file system recommends FSx for NetApp ONTAP when your current storage technology is NetApp ONTAP or another NAS appliance.
cards.scope: FSx file system choice by current storage technology.

cards.claim: The AWS page on choosing an FSx file system recommends FSx for OpenZFS when your current storage technology is ZFS or another Linux-based file server.
cards.scope: FSx file system choice by current storage technology.

cards.claim: The AWS page on choosing an FSx file system recommends FSx for Windows File Server when your current storage technology is Microsoft Windows Server.
cards.scope: FSx file system choice by current storage technology.

cards.claim: FSx for Windows File Server gives file- and folder-level access control with Windows ACLs, file system-level access control with VPC security groups, and API-level access control with IAM policies, and users are authenticated with Microsoft Active Directory.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server.

cards.claim: Amazon FSx does not support Active Directory Connector and Simple Active Directory.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server.

cards.claim: You can join an FSx for Windows File Server file system to AWS Managed Microsoft AD or to your existing self-managed Active Directory domain, on-premises or in the cloud.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server.

cards.claim: Automatic daily backups of an FSx for Windows File Server file system are deleted when the file system is deleted.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server backups.

cards.claim: You can automatically increase an FSx for Windows File Server file system's storage capacity when free storage capacity falls below a threshold that you specify, by deploying the AWS-developed custom CloudFormation template that implements the automated solution.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server storage capacity.

cards.claim: For FSx for Windows File Server you can use AWS Backup as part of a centralized backup solution for your AWS resources.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server backups.

cards.claim: During an FSx for Windows File Server backup, storage I/O may be suspended briefly, typically for a few seconds; because the VSS service needs to flush any cached writes to disk before resuming I/O, the pause may be longer when the workload has many write operations per second.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server backups.

cards.claim: You can use Amazon FSx to copy FSx for Windows File Server backups within the same account to another Region or within the same Region (cross-Region copies only within the same AWS partition), and you can use AWS Backup to copy backups across Regions and across accounts.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server backups.

cards.claim: When you create an FSx for Windows file system in the Amazon FSx console, the default automatic daily backup retention period is 30 days.
cards.scope: per file system, created in the Amazon FSx console; default; adjustable; the default differs in the Amazon FSx API and CLI.

cards.claim: You can set the automatic daily backup retention period of an FSx for Windows file system to be between 0–90 days.
cards.scope: per file system; maximum; adjustable.

cards.claim: Setting the retention period to 0 (zero) days turns off automatic daily backups of an FSx for Windows file system.
cards.scope: per file system.

cards.claim: FSx for Windows File Server backups are file-system-consistent (using VSS), highly durable and incremental, and Amazon FSx stores them in Amazon S3.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server backups.

cards.claim: For FSx for Windows File Server with a self-managed Active Directory, FSx rejoins the file server to Active Directory during failure recovery, routine maintenance and throughput capacity updates. If the Active Directory configuration is not valid during such an event, the file system changes to the Misconfigured status and is at risk of becoming unavailable.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server self-managed Active Directory.

cards.claim: FSx for Windows File Server requires that the SYSTEM user have full control NTFS ACL permissions on all folders in the file system; changing them may make the file system inaccessible and future backups unusable.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server NTFS ACLs.
links: [full control NTFS ACL permissions on all folders](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-bp-dont-change-system-user-ntfs-permissions)

cards.claim: AWS says not to modify or delete the elastic network interface (ENI) that is associated with an FSx for Windows File Server file system, because doing so can cause a permanent loss of connection between your VPC and the file system.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server network security.

cards.claim: You can join an FSx for Windows File Server file system to your Microsoft Active Directory domain to provide user authentication and share-, file- and folder-level access control. FSx provides two Active Directory options: AWS managed Microsoft Active Directory or self-managed Microsoft Active Directory.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server Active Directory.

cards.claim: AWS recommends keeping at least 20% of free storage capacity at all times on an FSx for Windows File Server file system, and increasing throughput capacity by at least 20% before increasing storage capacity to offset any performance impact during the storage increase.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server capacity planning.
links: [at least 20% of free storage capacity at all times](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-bp-keep-20-percent-free-storage)

cards.claim: You can use the FreeStorageCapacity CloudWatch metric to monitor the amount of free storage available on an FSx for Windows File Server file system and see how it trends.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server monitoring.

cards.claim: AWS recommends Multi-AZ file systems for most FSx for Windows File Server production workloads that require high availability to shared Windows file data.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server deployment types.

cards.claim: You can use AWS Secrets Manager to store and manage the Microsoft Active Directory domain join service account credentials for FSx for Windows File Server, which removes the need to store sensitive credentials in plaintext in application code or configuration files.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server self-managed Active Directory.

cards.claim: You can use security groups and network access control lists (ACLs) to limit access to FSx for Windows File Server file systems, and the security group and network ACLs for the subnets must allow traffic on the required ports.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server network security.
links: [security groups and network access control lists (ACLs)](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-bp-security-groups-and-network-acls-limit-access)

cards.claim: For FSx for Windows File Server with a self-managed Active Directory, AWS recommends a separate Organizational Unit for the file systems and a service account configured with the minimum privileges required.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server self-managed Active Directory.

cards.claim: If you use shadow copies on FSx for Windows File Server, AWS recommends increasing throughput capacity to a value at least three times the value that your workload is expected to drive, to avoid Windows Server deleting your shadow copies.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server shadow copies.

cards.claim: Updating throughput capacity of an FSx for Windows File Server file system interrupts availability for a few minutes on Single-AZ file systems and causes failover and failback on Multi-AZ file systems, so AWS recommends doing it during idle periods.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server throughput capacity updates.

cards.claim: FSx for Windows File Server uses standard Windows access control lists (ACLs) for fine-grained share-, file- and folder-level access control, and automatically verifies the credentials of users who access file system data to enforce them. You can migrate an existing security ACL configuration without modifications.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server access control.

cards.claim: For Microsoft SQL Server, FSx for Windows File Server supports continuously available (CA) file shares. You can create CA shares on Single-AZ 2 file systems, but it is required that you use CA shares on Multi-AZ file systems for all SQL Server deployments, whether HA or not.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server with Microsoft SQL Server.

cards.claim: You can access FSx for Windows File Server shares from all Windows versions starting from Windows Server 2008 and Windows 7 and from current versions of Linux, and you can map them on EC2 instances, WorkSpaces instances, AppStream 2.0 instances and VMware Cloud on AWS VMs.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server clients.

cards.claim: Data deduplication on FSx for Windows File Server runs as a background process that is transparent to users, and when you enable it data compression is enabled by default.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server data deduplication.

cards.claim: Data deduplication on FSx for Windows File Server typically saves 50 to 60 percent for general-purpose file shares, with 30 to 50 percent for user documents and 70 to 80 percent for software development datasets.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server data deduplication.

cards.claim: With Microsoft DFS Namespaces you can group file shares on multiple FSx for Windows File Server file systems into one namespace and scale file storage beyond the 64 TiB maximum of a single file system, up to hundreds of petabytes.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server DFS Namespaces.
links: [maximum storage capacity of single file system (64 TiB)](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-dfs-namespaces-group-file-systems-scale-beyond-64-tib)

cards.claim: By using DFS Namespaces you can scale out read and write performance for I/O-intensive workloads by spreading file data (shards) across multiple FSx file systems under one unified namespace.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server DFS Namespaces.

cards.claim: Using DNS aliases, you can move Windows file share data to FSx for Windows File Server and continue to use the existing DNS names to access the data.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server DNS aliases.

cards.claim: Amazon FSx registers DNS records for an FSx for Windows File Server file system only if you are using Microsoft DNS as the default DNS; if you are using a third-party DNS, you must manually set up DNS entries for your file systems.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server.
links: [only registers DNS records for a file system](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-dns-name-per-file-system-microsoft-dns)

cards.claim: All Amazon FSx file systems are encrypted at rest with keys managed in AWS KMS, using the AES-256 algorithm, and data is encrypted and decrypted transparently.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server encryption.

cards.claim: Data in transit to FSx for Windows File Server is automatically encrypted using SMB Kerberos session keys.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server encryption.

cards.claim: While a Multi-AZ file system fails over and back, I/O may be paused and CloudWatch metrics may be temporarily unavailable, and synchronizing activity during that time can take up to multiple hours for HDD storage and for write-heavy, IOPS-heavy workloads.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ.

cards.claim: Because the file system's DNS name stays the same, failovers are transparent to Windows applications, which resume file system operations without manual intervention.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ.

cards.claim: A Multi-AZ FSx for Windows file system fails over automatically from the preferred to the standby file server when an Availability Zone outage occurs, when the preferred file server becomes unavailable, or when it undergoes planned maintenance.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ.

cards.claim: A failover of a Multi-AZ FSx for Windows file system typically completes in less than 30 seconds, and failback to the preferred file server is automatic and also takes less than 30 seconds once the preferred file server has recovered.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ.

cards.claim: The FSx for Windows File Server FAQ says the service was designed for use cases that need Windows shared file storage, such as CRM, ERP, custom or .NET applications, home directories, web serving and content management, and Microsoft SQL Server.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server.

cards.claim: Amazon FSx File Gateway is no longer available to new customers, and existing customers can continue to use it normally.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx File Gateway.

cards.claim: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server provides fully managed Microsoft Windows file servers backed by a fully native Windows file system, and it supports the SMB protocol to access file storage over a network.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server.

cards.claim: When you create an FSx for Windows File Server file system you join it to your Active Directory domain, which provides user authentication and file- and folder-level access control.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server.
links: [user authentication and file- and folder-level access control](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-joins-active-directory-for-authentication-and-acls)

cards.claim: AWS recommends keeping at least 20% of free storage capacity on an FSx for Windows File Server file system at all times, because using all of it can hurt performance and might introduce data inconsistencies.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server storage capacity.

cards.claim: FSx for Windows File Server file servers use a fast in-memory cache to achieve consistent sub-millisecond latencies for actively accessed data.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server, data in the in-memory cache.

cards.claim: For data not in the in-memory cache, FSx for Windows File Server provides sub-millisecond file operation latencies with SSD storage and single-digit millisecond latencies with HDD storage.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server, data not in the in-memory cache.

cards.claim: The maximum retention period for automated backups of an FSx for Windows File Server file system is 90 days.
cards.scope: per file system; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: The maximum number of backup copy requests in progress to a single destination Region per account is 5.
cards.scope: per account, per destination Region; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: The maximum number of file shares of an FSx for Windows File Server file system is 100,000.
cards.scope: per file system; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: The maximum SSD IOPS of an FSx for Windows File Server file system is 400,000; FSx file systems provide 400,000 IOPS in US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), US East (Ohio), Europe (Ireland), Asia Pacific (Tokyo) and Asia Pacific (Singapore), and up to 80,000 IOPS in all AWS Regions where Amazon FSx is available.
cards.scope: per file system; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: The maximum storage capacity of an FSx for Windows SSD or HDD file system is 64 TiB.
cards.scope: per file system, SSD and HDD; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: The maximum throughput capacity of an FSx for Windows File Server file system is 12,288 MBps; throughput capacity levels of 4,608 MBps and higher are supported only in US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), US East (Ohio), Europe (Ireland), Asia Pacific (Tokyo) and Asia Pacific (Singapore).
cards.scope: per file system; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: The minimum storage capacity of an FSx for Windows HDD file system is 2,000 GiB.
cards.scope: per HDD file system; minimum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: The minimum storage capacity of an FSx for Windows SSD file system is 32 GiB.
cards.scope: per SSD file system; minimum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: The minimum SSD IOPS of an FSx for Windows File Server file system is 96.
cards.scope: per file system; minimum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: The minimum throughput capacity of an FSx for Windows File Server file system is 8 MBps.
cards.scope: per file system; minimum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: The maximum number of tags per FSx for Windows File Server file system is 50.
cards.scope: per file system; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: Linux clients do not support automatic DNS-based failover, so they don't automatically connect to the standby file server during a failover; they automatically resume file system operations after the Multi-AZ file system has failed back to the file server in the preferred subnet.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ.

cards.claim: If you connect an FSx for Windows File Server file system to an AWS Managed Microsoft AD in a different VPC or account, you must ensure connectivity between that VPC and the VPC where you create the file system.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server.

cards.claim: To migrate large amounts of data to FSx for Windows File Server as quickly as possible, use a file system configured with SSD storage, and afterwards you can move the data to HDD storage if that suits your application.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server migration.

cards.claim: To migrate existing files to FSx for Windows File Server, AWS recommends AWS DataSync, and as an alternative you can use Robocopy.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server migration.
links: [you can use Robust File Copy, or Robocopy](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-migrate-with-datasync-or-robocopy)

cards.claim: Compared with Single-AZ, Multi-AZ deployments give enhanced durability by replicating data across AZs, and enhanced availability by failing over automatically to the standby AZ during planned maintenance and unplanned disruption.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ.
links: [enhanced durability by further replicating data across AZs](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-multi-az-enhanced-durability-availability-auto-failover)

cards.claim: In the feature support table for FSx for Windows File Server, the Multi-AZ deployment type is marked for SSD storage, HDD storage, DFS namespaces, custom DNS names and CA shares, and has no mark for DFS replication; a note on the CA shares mark says you should use CA shares on Multi-AZ file systems for SQL Server HA deployments.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server deployment type.

cards.claim: AWS recommends Multi-AZ file systems for most production workloads, and describes Single-AZ as a cost-efficient solution for test and development workloads and for production workloads with replication in the application layer or relaxed availability and RPO needs.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server deployment types.

cards.claim: A Multi-AZ FSx for Windows file system is a high-availability cluster of Windows file servers across two Availability Zones (a preferred and a standby AZ) using Windows Server Failover Clustering, and data is replicated synchronously within each AZ and between the two AZs.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ.

cards.claim: Other SMB-compatible clients may function with FSx for Windows File Server, but they are not supported by AWS.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server clients.
links: [may function but are not supported by AWS](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-other-smb-clients-not-supported-by-aws)

cards.claim: When you access an FSx for Windows File Server file system from the same Region but from an AZ other than its preferred AZ, Multi-AZ file systems created before February 23, 2022 and Single-AZ file systems are charged $0.01/GB in each direction.
cards.scope: per GB in each direction, access from a non-preferred AZ in the same Region; Multi-AZ file systems created before February 23, 2022, and Single-AZ file systems.

cards.claim: AWS says the cost of FSx for Windows File Server has five categories: storage capacity, SSD IOPS, throughput capacity, backups and data transfer.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server billing.

cards.claim: When you access an FSx for Windows File Server file system from the same Region but from an AZ other than its preferred AZ, Multi-AZ file systems created on or after February 23, 2022 have no data transfer charges.
cards.scope: Multi-AZ file systems created on or after February 23, 2022.

cards.claim: For FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ file systems, the cost of transferring data between Availability Zones for replication is included in the throughput capacity price.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ billing.

cards.claim: For FSx for Windows File Server, pricing is quoted on a monthly basis, usage is prorated by the hour, and you are billed for your average usage over a month.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server.

cards.claim: FSx for Windows File Server includes 3 IOPS for every GB of SSD storage by default; you can optionally provision more and pay for the average IOPS provisioned above the included rate.
cards.scope: per GB of SSD storage; default; adjustable; you can provision a higher level of IOPS.
links: [3 IOPS are included for every GB of SSD storage](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-pricing-ssd-iops-3-per-gb-included)

cards.claim: The FSx for Windows File Server price of storage capacity depends on the deployment type (single-AZ or multi-AZ) and the storage type (SSD or HDD) you choose.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server storage capacity.

cards.claim: The FSx for Windows File Server price of throughput capacity depends on the deployment type (single-AZ or multi-AZ) you choose for your file system.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server throughput capacity.

cards.claim: The default for Windows backups is 500, the maximum number of user-initiated backups for all FSx for Windows File Server file systems that you can have in this account.
cards.scope: per account, per AWS Region, all Windows file systems; default; adjustable.

cards.claim: The default for Windows file systems is 100, the maximum number of Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file systems that you can create in this account.
cards.scope: per account, per AWS Region; default; adjustable.

cards.claim: The default for Windows HDD storage capacity is 524288, the maximum amount of HDD storage capacity (in GiB) allowed for all FSx for Windows File Server file systems in this account.
cards.scope: per account, per AWS Region, all Windows file systems; default; adjustable.

cards.claim: The default for Windows SSD storage capacity is 524288, the maximum amount of SSD storage capacity (in GiB) allowed for all FSx for Windows File Server file systems in this account.
cards.scope: per account, per AWS Region, all Windows file systems; default; adjustable.

cards.claim: The default for Windows throughput capacity is 10240, the total amount of throughput capacity (in MBps) allowed for all Amazon FSx for Windows file systems in this account.
cards.scope: per account, per AWS Region, all Windows file systems; default; adjustable.

cards.claim: The default for Windows total SSD IOPS is 500,000, the total amount of SSD IOPS allowed for all FSx for Windows File Server file systems in this account.
cards.scope: per account, per AWS Region, all Windows file systems; default; adjustable.

cards.claim: In the resource forest isolation model, you join your FSx for Windows File Server file system to an AWS Managed Microsoft AD setup and then establish a one-way forest trust relationship between that AWS Managed Microsoft AD domain and your existing self-managed Active Directory domain.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server.

cards.claim: When you enable shadow copies on FSx for Windows, the default limit for the maximum number of shadow copies stored on the file system is 20.
cards.scope: per file system; default; adjustable; you can set it up to 500.

cards.claim: You can store a maximum of 500 shadow copies per file system at any point in time on FSx for Windows; fewer than 64 are recommended.
cards.scope: per file system; maximum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: Shadow copies are not enabled on FSx for Windows File Server by default; to protect your data with shadow copies you must enable shadow copies and set up a shadow copy schedule, and shadow copies are not a substitute for backups.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server shadow copies; default; adjustable.

cards.claim: A Microsoft Windows shadow copy is a snapshot of a Windows file system at a point in time, and with shadow copies enabled users can quickly recover deleted or changed files and compare file versions.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server shadow copies.

cards.claim: When you enable shadow copies on FSx for Windows, the default limit for the maximum shadow copy storage is 10 percent of your file system.
cards.scope: per file system; default; adjustable.

cards.claim: In the feature support table for FSx for Windows File Server, the Single-AZ 1 deployment type is marked for SSD storage, DFS namespaces, DFS replication and custom DNS names, and has no mark for HDD storage or CA shares.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server deployment type.

cards.claim: In the feature support table for FSx for Windows File Server, the Single-AZ 2 deployment type is marked for SSD storage, HDD storage, DFS namespaces, custom DNS names and CA shares, and has no mark for DFS replication; a note on the CA shares mark says that while you can create CA shares on Single-AZ 2 file systems, you should use CA shares on Multi-AZ file systems for SQL Server HA deployments.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server deployment type.

cards.claim: A Single-AZ FSx for Windows file system has one Windows file server and its storage volumes in a single Availability Zone, replicates data automatically against the failure of a single component in most cases, and usually has about 30 minutes of downtime during failure recovery and planned maintenance.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server Single-AZ.

cards.claim: With a Single-AZ FSx for Windows file system, failure may be unrecoverable in rare cases, such as multiple component failures or a non-graceful failure of the single file server, in which case you recover from the most recent backup.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server Single-AZ.

cards.claim: FSx for Windows File Server is compatible with the SMB protocol versions 2.0 through 3.1.1.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server.

cards.claim: You can use FSx for Windows File Server as shared storage for high availability SQL Server in two ways, as storage for active data files and as an SMB file share witness, and SSD storage is recommended for SQL Server.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server with SQL Server.

cards.claim: AWS recommends SSD storage for SQL Server on FSx for Windows File Server, because SSD storage is designed for the highest-performance and most latency-sensitive workloads, including databases.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server with Microsoft SQL Server.

cards.claim: In Automatic mode, Amazon FSx automatically scales the SSD IOPS of an FSx for Windows file system to maintain 3 SSD IOPS per GiB of storage capacity, up to 400,000 SSD IOPS per file system.
cards.scope: per FSx for Windows file system, Automatic IOPS mode; default; adjustable; up to 400,000 SSD IOPS per file system.

cards.claim: For higher levels of provisioned SSD IOPS on FSx for Windows, you pay for the average IOPS above 3 IOPS per GiB per file system.
cards.scope: per FSx for Windows file system.

cards.claim: In User-provisioned mode you can specify the number of SSD IOPS of an FSx for Windows file system within the range of 96–400,000.
cards.scope: per FSx for Windows file system, User-provisioned IOPS mode; maximum; adjustable.

cards.claim: You cannot make further storage capacity increases on an FSx for Windows File Server file system until 6 hours after the last increase was requested or until storage optimization has completed, whichever is longer.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server storage capacity.
links: [6 hours after the last increase was requested](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-storage-capacity-6-hours-between-increases)

cards.claim: Each storage capacity increase of an FSx for Windows File Server file system must be a minimum of 10 percent of the current storage capacity, up to the maximum allowed value of 65,536 GiB.
cards.scope: per storage capacity increase, FSx for Windows File Server; minimum; not adjustable.

cards.claim: You can only increase the storage capacity of an FSx for Windows File Server file system; you cannot decrease it.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server storage capacity.

cards.claim: FSx for Windows File Server offers SSD and HDD storage; HDD is designed for home directories, user and departmental shares and content management systems, and SSD for the highest-performance, most latency-sensitive workloads such as databases, media processing and data analytics.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server storage types.

cards.claim: To increase storage capacity, an FSx for Windows file system must have a minimum throughput capacity of 16 MBps.
cards.scope: per FSx for Windows file system; minimum; to increase storage capacity.

cards.claim: You can change the storage type of an FSx for Windows File Server file system from HDD to SSD but not from SSD to HDD; to go from SSD to HDD you restore a backup to a new file system that uses HDD storage.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server storage type.

cards.claim: FSx for Windows File Server is supported for Amazon EC2 instances, including Microsoft Windows, Mac, and Amazon Linux 2023 instances, and for Amazon ECS containers.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server clients.

cards.claim: You can test failover of a Multi-AZ FSx for Windows file system by modifying its throughput capacity.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ.

cards.claim: Throughput capacity levels of 4,608 MBps and higher are supported only in US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), US East (Ohio), Europe (Ireland), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Asia Pacific (Singapore).
cards.scope: per FSx for Windows file system; minimum; supported only in six listed Regions.

cards.claim: Throughput capacity levels below 32 megabytes per second (MBps) can be selected with the Amazon FSx API or CLI, but they are meant for test and development workloads, not for production workloads.
cards.scope: per FSx for Windows file system.

cards.claim: Amazon FSx file systems provide up to 2 GBps and 80,000 IOPS in all AWS Regions where Amazon FSx is available, and 12 GBps of throughput and 400,000 IOPS in US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), US East (Ohio), Europe (Ireland), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Asia Pacific (Singapore).
cards.scope: per FSx for Windows file system, by AWS Region; maximum; not adjustable; the 12 GBps and 400,000 IOPS levels apply in six listed Regions.

cards.claim: User-initiated FSx for Windows File Server backups never expire, are available for as long as you want to keep them, and are retained even after you delete the file system that was backed up.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server backups.
links: [backups of Amazon FSx file systems never expire](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-user-initiated-backups-never-expire)
[retained even after you delete the file system](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-user-initiated-backups-never-expire)

cards.claim: FSx for Windows File Server supports VPC sharing, which enables you to view, create, modify and delete resources in a shared subnet in a VPC owned by another AWS account.
cards.scope: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server.

cards.claim: You can access FSx for Windows File Server file shares from on-premises compute instances using AWS Direct Connect or Site-to-Site VPN, and from a different VPC, account or AWS Region using VPC peering or transit gateways.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server network access.

cards.claim: FSx for Windows File Server is accessible with the SMB protocol, supporting versions 2.0 to 3.1.1, from all Windows versions starting from Windows Server 2008 and Windows 7, and also from current versions of Linux.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server.

cards.claim: AWS says that with file storage on Amazon FSx the code, applications and tools that Windows developers and administrators use today can continue to work unchanged. Ideal workloads include business applications, home directories, web serving, content management, data analytics, software build setups and media processing.
cards.scope: FSx for Windows File Server.
